chapters.summary: Susan Zhuang begins by noting a tradition of showing photos from senior centers, but says many centers are afraid to submit pictures. She introduces herself as Chair of the Aging Committee and thanks attendees for the oversight hearing on older adult centers in NYCHA facilities. She thanks co-chair Chris Banks.
chapters.title: Chair Susan Zhuang opens Aging Committee remarks and notes senior center photo tradition

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And we know we have a tradition.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Start this year, we're going to have pictures showing some situation in all the senior centers.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, good morning.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I'm Councilmember Susan Zhuang, Chair of the New York City Council's Committee on Aging.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I want to thank you all for being here today for this important oversight hearing on older adult centers in night shift facilities.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I want to thank my co-chair, Councilmember Banks of the Committee of Public Housing for agreeing to hold this hearing with me for thousands of older adults in New York City.

chapters.summary: Zhuang says OACs provide hot meals, community, and physical and mental well-being. Staff and caseworkers help with services, deed theft education, and elder abuse prevention. She emphasizes these centers help older adults live safely.
chapters.title: Zhuang describes vital services provided by older adult centers

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Older adult centers or OACs provide

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: vital services.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: They offer hot meals, provide a sense of community, and promote physical and mental well-being.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Beyond that, the dedicated staff and the caseworkers employed at OACs assist older adults in assisting services, provide education on deed theft

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: and older abuse, and they ensure that each older adult

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: They work equipped with knowledge they need to live safely and securely.

chapters.summary: Zhuang says OACs face unique challenges when aging infrastructure fails, especially in NYCHA properties. Leaking roofs, failing pipes, HVAC systems, and fire panels disrupt services and can threaten safety. Providers often struggle to remain open.
chapters.title: Zhuang outlines infrastructure failures at NYCHA older adult centers

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: However, OACs face a number of unique challenges.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: When things break, when aging infrastructure finally begins to fail, repairs can often take substantial time.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: In that time, OACs may struggle to provide services older adults rely on, if they are able to remain open at all.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And for OACs that operate in NITCHA property, this issue especially occurred.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I know NITCHA has long-standing infrastructure challenges, which I'm sure my co-chair will touch on.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: These issues often extend to the facility provided by NITCHA to OAC providers.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Leaking roof, failing pipe, failing HVAC system, or even

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: fire panel which are not maintained, all those issues cause disruption and the extremely cases can even present a direct threat to service recipient safety.

chapters.summary: Zhuang says providers report an unclear division of labor between NYCHA and DFTA when repairs are needed. Some are left to handle damage like burst pipes through their own fundraising. She notes providers can face FDNY fines for unsafe conditions they cannot repair.
chapters.title: Zhuang says repair process between NYCHA and DFTA is unclear

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: OAC providers have told us

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: When those issues rise, the process for addressing them is unclear.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: The division of labor between NITRA and the DFTA is blurry.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And that they are sometimes left to deal with those issues, such as damage from burst pipe.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: On their own through, they have to do their own fundraising.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Furthermore, OAC providers can even find themselves facing fines from agencies like FDNY because failing infrastructure, which they are often not allowed to repair on their own.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Has left their facility fundamentally unsafe, and that is a big issue.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I'm sure we can all agree that an OAC provider should never be struggled on an oath court hearing because NYCHA and the DFTA have not...

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Remanded a critical infrastructure failure.

chapters.summary: Zhuang says the hearing aims to clarify how OAC providers can get needed repairs and where collaboration has failed. She thanks Commissioner Lisa Scott McKenzie and COO Eva Trimble for attending. She looks forward to hearing how the council can help agencies overcome hurdles.
chapters.title: Zhuang calls for clarity on OAC repairs and agency collaboration

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We are here today to provide clarity for OAC providers located in

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: facility on the process for getting those such needed repairs and to hear from agencies themselves where collaboration has failed, where this is working, and what improvement can be

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: need to be made.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: The council and the committees look forward to hearing how we can assist the agency in clear whatever hurdles they are facing.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And I want to thank both Commissioner Dr.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Lisa Scott McKenzie and Chief Operator Officer Eva Trimble for being here today.

chapters.summary: Zhuang describes Intro 1083, sponsored by Councilmember Hudson, which would require a financial literacy advisor in each OAC for at least 20 hours a month. Advisors would provide information on financial literacy, end-of-life preparation, taxes, and avoiding scams. She thanks Hudson for her leadership.
chapters.title: Zhuang highlights Intro 1083 on financial literacy advisors

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Before I pass the mic to my co-chair, I also want to highlight the bill we are hearing today, Intro 1083, sponsored by Councilmember Hudson, could require

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Commissioner of Agent to designate at least one financial literacy advisor to serve in each OAC for at least 20 hours a month.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: This advisor would provide older adults general information about financial literacy,

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: end-of-life preparation, tax preparation, and how to avoid and handle legal issues and a scam which commonly affect older adults.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: This is often overlooked issue, and I want to thank my colleague, Councilmember Hudson, for her leadership on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I also want to thank the

chapters.summary: Zhuang thanks her staff and committee staff for preparing the hearing. She recognizes Council Members Anna Strong, Marte, and others attending in person or on Zoom. She then yields to co-chair Chris Banks.
chapters.title: Zhuang thanks staff and recognizes attending council members

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I want to thank my staff, Jennifer Somp-Moscon, Jade Nash, and the committee staff, Amita Klawan,

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Josh Newman, Julia Harms, Margaret

utterances.text: Bursley and Colby Porter for their work in preparing for today's hearing.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: If I mispronounce anyone's name wrong, please forgive me.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I would also like to recognize the following council members who have joined here today.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Council Member Anna Strong.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And Canarsie and Councilmember Marte and then Abdul.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And then Areola on the Zoom.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Now I give the floor to my co-chair, Councilmember Banks, for his opening remark.

chapters.summary: Banks thanks Chair Zhuang and welcomes attendees to the joint hearing. He introduces himself as Chair of the Public Housing Committee. He says older adult centers are critically important for thousands of older New Yorkers, especially public housing residents.
chapters.title: Chair Chris Banks opens Public Housing Committee remarks on OACs

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair Swong, and good morning to everyone, and welcome to this joint hearing.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I am Councilmember Chris Vanks, Chair of the Public Housing Committee, and I would like to also again thank Chair Swong for co-chairing this important hearing with me.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Older adult centers are critically important to provide

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I'm sorry, older adult centers are critically important provider for thousands of older New Yorkers, especially those residing in public housing.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: They provide essential social services while also serving as a regular touch point of community and otherwise are crucial to contributions to improving older residents'quality of life.

chapters.summary: Banks says OACs are forced to provide services in neglected and disrepair conditions. He lists leaking ceilings, broken elevators, pest problems, mold, outdated kitchens and bathrooms. These conditions sometimes force OAC services to be suspended or halted.
chapters.title: Banks details poor conditions at NYCHA older adult centers

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: However, the older adult centers have been forced to provide services in far less than ideal conditions.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And with NITRA facilities, they are used to being consistently neglected or in disrepair.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Leaking ceilings, broken elevators, pest problems, mold issues.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: outdated kitchens and bathrooms and more have not only affected the older adult centers, but also the residents receiving their services.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Often the conditions are so bad that the OAC services have to be suspended or halted altogether.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Leaving both providers and recipients in limbo as they wait for repairs.

chapters.summary: Banks says NYCHA has a poor track record maintaining buildings, including facilities used by OACs. While NYCHA has been under federal monitorship since 2019 for residential habitability, there is no such monitor for commercial facilities leased to community providers. He has heard countless complaints about persistent repair problems.
chapters.title: Banks says NYCHA lacks oversight for commercial facilities leased to OACs

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: NITRA, unfortunately, does not have a good track record when it comes to maintaining its buildings.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And this extends to their facilities that are used by the older adult centers.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Importantly, while NYCHA has been under federal monitorship since 2019

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: to improve its operations and facilitate a baseline standard of hability for NYCHA residents,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: it has no such monitor when it comes to its commercial facilities that get leased to community service providers like the OACs.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And I've received and have heard of countless complaints around the persistent problems that these

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: older adult centers and older residents face because of NYCHA's lack of timely, timely, transparent operations when it comes to repairs.

chapters.summary: Banks says lack of clear communication about NYCHA versus OAC responsibility causes delays. Some OACs pay for repairs themselves to resume services instead of waiting months for NYCHA. He appreciates NYCHA's stated efforts but says actions must deliver.
chapters.title: Banks criticizes unclear repair responsibilities and providers paying out of pocket

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Further compounding this issue is the lack of clear communication on what is NITRA's responsibility versus what is the OAC's responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: for facility management, leading to additional delays.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And it has gotten to the point where the older adult centers result to paying for repairs out of their own pocket

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: just to resume providing their services to the community instead of waiting on NYCHA for more months.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You know, I'm aware that NYCHA is endeavoring to improve its operations, and I appreciate that we all share the same goal in providing communal benefit for NYCHA residents.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: But sentiment only goes so far when actions fails to deliver.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Especially when the population impacted are our older adults, where the efforts of delays are magnified and when residents'trust is low, thanks to issues surrounding the PAC conversion process.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: We must push for more clarity and transparency so that we can all be on the same page.

chapters.summary: Banks says the hearing should establish clarity on how OACs can get timely repairs from NYCHA. He wants to understand the distinction between DFTA and NYCHA responsibilities and what can be done now for immediate relief. He also wants to hear how NYCHA handles repairs during PACT conversions.
chapters.title: Banks outlines hearing goals on repairs, PAC conversions, and immediate relief

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Today's hearing is important for several reasons, not the least of which is establishing with definitive clarity how the OACs can ensure more timely repairs from NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And the distinction between DIFTA's and NYCHA's responsibility.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I am intent on finding out

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I, NITRA, continues to struggle with meeting the needs of its older residents and with issuing clear lines of communication.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Despite previous council hearings on this issue and legislation creating a liaison, I'm also keen on the understanding of what can be done now to have more immediate relief.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: For the issues presently plaguing the OACs at NYCHA, and what we can do so that moving forward, the older adult centers do not have to bear the undue burden

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: of repairs and can dedicate their focus on their original purpose, which is serving the older adult population.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: This hearing will also be a chance to hear how NYCHA is handling the facility repairs and related communications when it comes to developments undergoing and completing PAC conversions.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I look forward to hearing from NITRA, DFTA, and those present today to gather more insight on this issue.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I want to also continue to work together with the older adults and the older NITRA adult residents

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: so that they can live lives with dignity, community, instead of with confusion and hostility.

chapters.summary: Banks thanks his staff Michael Lambert, Kyle Graham, and committee staff Jose, Samia, Charles, Spencer, James, and Noah. He says he wants to work together so older NYCHA residents can live with dignity and community.
chapters.title: Banks thanks Public Housing Committee staff

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I would also like to thank my staff, Michael Lambert, Kyle Graham, and along with the Public Housing Committee.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Staff, Jose, Samia, Charles, Spencer, James, Noah, for all the hard work that you've put in in making this hearing, putting into this hearing.

chapters.title: Zhuang transitions to public panel of older adults and NYCHA residents

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, thank you, my co-chair, Chris Banks, Councilmember Chris Banks.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Now we will hear from pre-panel order adults, NITRA residents.

chapters.summary: Sarah Morgage testifies as a board member of Riverstone Senior Life Services. She notes she previously worked for Councilmember Robert Jackson and now works at Literacy and Community. She describes Riverstone's location in Washington Heights and its engaging older adult programming.
chapters.title: Sarah Morgage introduces Riverstone Senior Life Services

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: And good morning.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: Thank you for the opportunity to present testimony today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: My name is Sarah Morgage, and I'm speaking as a board member of Riverstone Senior Life Services.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: Some of you may already know me as a staff member to Robert Jackson for the 12 years he served as a council member.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: I currently work as the Senior Manager for Advancement at Literacy and Community, or LINK, where we provide early literacy programming for families with children from birth through five years, so kind of the opposite end of life's bell curve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: Link is the backbone partner for Cities First Readers, the Council's only early literacy initiative.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: Full disclosure, several members of these committees support Link, and that funding is deeply appreciated.

chapters.summary: Morgage says Riverstone offers art classes, pool tables, social services, and a health homes program. It uniquely operates the borough's only bilingual adult day program for dementia. Riverstone turns 40 this year and has been housed at NYCHA's Senior Development at 99 Fort Washington Avenue the whole time.
chapters.title: Morgage describes Riverstone programs and 40-year history at NYCHA

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: Riverstone is located in Washington Heights and provides really engaging older adult center programming.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: The art classes are fabulous.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: The center vibrates with energy, but to tell you the truth, I think it's the pool tables that bring in more men than is usual at a senior center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: There is a very effective social services department and a vital health homes program.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: Uniquely, Riverstone also operates the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: Burroughs only bilingual adult day program for those with dementia or other memory impairments.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: We would welcome a visit from any of you on these committees to see our programs in action.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: Riverstone turns 40 this year.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: And has been housed at NYCHA's Senior Development, 99 Fort Washington Avenue, the whole time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: I joined the board in 2016, but I was also involved with Riverstone through my council staff responsibilities from 2002 to 2013.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: So I think I

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: have a good background view of the organization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: Under NYCHA management, we had a fairly typical nonprofit experience, including no rent since we were a mandated service to support a senior housing development.

chapters.summary: Morgage explains that under NYCHA management, Riverstone had no rent as a mandated service. Under RAD, the landlord is now a private developer, Pact Renaissance Corporation. She says the relationship has been contentious and nonprofit providers are an afterthought.
chapters.title: Morgage says RAD program shifted Riverstone's landlord to private developer

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: But under the RAD program,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: things have shifted dramatically.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: So our issue is slightly different than what has been described because our landlord is not NYCHA, but a private developer.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: So our written testimony that will be submitted later today will provide a lot more detail, but I want to emphasize four things today.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: First, we understand that

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: RAD is intended to benefit the residents.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: The nonprofit service providers are clearly an afterthought.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: I suspect many are individually, many other older adult centers or nonprofit service providers in RAD buildings

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: are individually encountering similar challenges as Riverstone is.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: Item two, our relationship with our for-profit developer, Pact Renaissance Corporation, or PRC, has been contentious for many reasons.

chapters.summary: Morgage says PRC caused water damage and insisted repairs be claimed against Riverstone's policy. This led to dropped coverage and a deductible increase from $1,000 to $25,000 per incident. Riverstone was without property liability insurance from November 25 through February 26, and later coverage was canceled due to illegal fire panels PRC refused to remove.
chapters.title: Morgage details loss of property liability insurance due to PRC disputes

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: Among the issues we've faced, they have caused us to lose our property liability coverage twice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: As a board member, operating without insurance is a very perilous situation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: The first time we lost coverage was because PRC insisted that repairs from water damage they caused

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: should be claimed against our policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: And when you start working in a building that hasn't been maintained for many years, leaks are inevitable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: Our coverage with a long-time vendor was dropped because of too many claims.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: For two years, PRC carried us under its own policy.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: We paid the premium, but our deductible soared from $1,000 per incident to $25,000.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: per incident.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: PRC refused to continue that arrangement and we were without property liability insurance from November 25 through February 26.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: The coverage we obtained then was canceled in May because

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: Outmoded and illegal fire panels were found in the ceiling.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: PRC has refused to remove them, which effectively keeps us from obtaining new coverage.

chapters.summary: Morgage says DFTA initially assured signing a lease was voluntary, but that was reversed and PRC is pressuring Riverstone. The agreement includes eviction if Riverstone fails to maintain insurance coverage, which PRC caused them to lose. She says the template from NYCHA appears framed for for-profit enterprises.
chapters.title: Morgage says PRC pressures Riverstone to sign unfavorable license agreement

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: Third point, after written assurances by DFTA that signing any lease was voluntary, that was

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: administratively reversed and PRC is pressuring us to sign a very unfavorable license agreement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: Ironically, one stipulation in that agreement is that Riverstone is subject to eviction if we fail to maintain required insurance coverage.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: So sit with that for just a minute.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: They cause us to lose our insurance.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: And then they can use that as justification for evicting us if we sign their agreement.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: There are numerous other onerous conditions, such as giving a for-profit contractor the right to change the name of the organization.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: PRC's license agreement template was provided by NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: and appears to be framed with for-profit enterprises in mind.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: There's a lot of language about not being able to operate a funeral parlor or a tattoo parlor or a liquor store.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: Our objections to the proposed provisions are numerous and they're spelled out in our written testimony.

chapters.summary: Morgage says the conflict has diverted staff and board time from running the older adult center. She describes PRC as a bottom-line enterprise that underbudgeted its Manhattan RAD properties. PRC once said it needed investor approval to replace a faulty HVAC system, so Riverstone paid for the repair.
chapters.title: Morgage says disputes divert resources and PRC underbudgeted RAD properties

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: Fourth point, all of this has diverted the time, the energy, and the resources of the staff and board from the normal challenges of running an older adult center and serving our community.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: It's been a stressful and combative experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: We are at the mercy of a very bottom line enterprise that has clearly under budgeted its Manhattan bundle of rad properties and has its profit margin as its main, if not only consideration.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: In fact, the PRC representative once told us that they would need to get the approval of their investors to replace a faulty HVAC system in the memory center.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: Riverstone paid for the repair, but surely HVAC comes under the heading of building systems and should be PRC's responsibility.

chapters.summary: Morgage thanks the committee and says she is happy to answer questions about Riverstone's experiences. She offers her organization's involvement in formulating next steps. Chair Zhuang thanks her.
chapters.title: Morgage offers to answer questions and help formulate next steps

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: I'm grateful for the opportunity to speak today, and I would be very happy to answer any questions you may have about our experiences.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: And I'd be very happy for our organization to be involved in formulating whatever next steps.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: steps take place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Sarah Morgage
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And the next we have Patricia Lynch.

chapters.summary: Patricia Lynch testifies as Older Adult Supervisor at Millennium Development. She says they operate three older adult centers in NYCHA facilities, with a fourth opening next month. She thanks Councilmember Banks and NYC Aging for supporting their programs.
chapters.title: Patricia Lynch introduces Millennium Development OACs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: How are you?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: Good morning, Councilmember Chris Banks and Duong, members of the Committee on Aging, New York City Aging Commissioner Dr.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: Scott McKenzie, and all distinguished members of New York City Council.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: My name is Patricia Lynch, and I am the Older Adult Supervisor at Millennium Development.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: We currently operate three older adult centers within NITRA facilities, with a fourth opening next month.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: First, I want to sincerely thank City Council Member Chris Banks and New York City Aging for always supporting our programs, and more importantly, for truly caring about the older adults we serve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: Your continued support and understanding of how important these centers are to our community is not going unnoticed, and I am grateful for the opportunity to speak today.

chapters.summary: Lynch says older adults come to centers for friendship, meals, activities, and belonging. She says centers work to feel like a second home but constantly deal with building issues with no clear resolution. Leaks and lack of heat force closures of sections and disrupt programming.
chapters.title: Lynch describes the importance of OACs and ongoing building issues

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: When I think about our older adult centers, I think about the people who walk through our doors every day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: People who have worked their entire lives, raised families, contributed to their communities, and now they're at a place where they can simply enjoy the chapter of their lives.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: For many of our older adults, the center is more than somewhere to go during the day.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: It's where they see their friends, share a meal, laugh, participate in activities, and feel like they belong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: For some, it may be the only part of the time of the day that they get to conversate with anyone or feel part of something.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: And that's why these centers mean so much to us.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: We work hard to make our centers feel like a second home, but how can we truly provide that feeling?

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: We are constantly dealing with building issues that seem to have no clear resolution.

chapters.summary: Lynch says the main challenge is lack of communication, accountability, and responsibility when problems arise. Providers make calls and emails, get directed from person to person, and time passes without resolution. She says someone must take responsibility for seeing an issue through to the end.
chapters.title: Lynch criticizes lack of communication and accountability for repairs

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: I want to be clear that the issues I'm raising today are not the only challenges we face, but they are concerns the most of overall lack of communication, accountability, and responsibility when problems arise.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: Something as simple as a leak become an ongoing issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: Every time it rains, we should not have to worry about water coming to a center where older adults are supposed to feel safe and comfortable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: We should not have to close those sections of the center because there is no key, leaving us to figure out how to continue programming while keeping our participants warm and comfortable.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: These are not luxuries we're asking for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: We're talking about basic conditions that every older adult deserves.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: And what makes these situations even more frustrating is that when we reach out for help, it often feels like no one wants to take ownership of the problem.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: We make phone calls and emails, follow up and try to get answers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: Sometimes we are directed from one person to another, and before we know it, so much time has passed and the original problem is still there.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: Even something as basic as putting a repair ticket can be difficult.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: We understand that buildings are older and repairs take time.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: We understand that there is a process that must be followed, but there needs to be more communication.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: There needs to be more follow through.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: And most importantly, there needs to be someone who takes responsibility for seeing an issue through the ends.

chapters.summary: Lynch says RAD/PACT transitions involve budgets and contracts, but the dollar amount can overshadow the people affected. Older adults do not see contracts or management companies; they only know their center is not what it should be. She says behind every repair request is a person.
chapters.title: Lynch says RAD/PACT transitions overlook human impact

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: I also want to speak about the RADPAC and the challenges that come with these transitions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: I understand that there are budget contracts and financial responsibilities involved in managing a program, but there sometimes feels like

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: It's overlooked in terms of the dollar amount.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: Instead of looking at the actual people, it's being affected.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: When an older adult walks into a center, they should not have to worry about whether the ceiling is going to be leaking when it rains or whether the room they're enjoying their activities will be closed because there is no heat.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: They don't see the contracts, the budgets, or the agency or the management company that are responsible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: They only know that the place they look forward to coming to every day is not what it should be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: And that is what we need everyone involved to remember.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: Behind every repair request is a person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: Behind every unresolved building issue are older adults who deserve better.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: Whether a building is managed by NITRO or through Red Pack, there should never be confusion about who is responsible for addressing these conditions.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: The responsibility should not be passed around while older adults continue to wait.

chapters.summary: Lynch says none of their current locations have a place of assembly, and many OACs in NYCHA facilities lack formal MOUs or leases. This affects their ability to make improvements, and capital projects can be delayed. OACs are often written up by NYC Aging and FDNY while older adults lose out.
chapters.title: Lynch says lack of MOUs and leases delays capital projects

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: Another challenge we face is none of the current locations have a place of assembly, and many of our older adult centers operating in NITRA facilities do not have formal MOUs or lease agreements in place.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: These issues may sound like paperwork or administrative matters, but they affect our ability to make improvements in our centers.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: Without proper agreements, capital projects can be delayed or cannot move forward, and OACs are often written up by New York City Aging and FDNY.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: And once again, our older adults are the ones who lose out.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: We see that our centers could be.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: We see the improvements that could be made.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: We see the potential to create a brighter, safer, and comfortable space.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: But too often, we find ourselves spending more time trying to navigate the system and getting answers than actually moving forward with these improvements.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: As providers, we want to focus our energy on the people we serve.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: We want to create programs that make them happy, keep them active, support their independence, and give them somewhere to look forward to.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: We should not have to spend so much time trying to fight the basic building issues and address these issues.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: Our staff should not have to constantly find ways to work around the problems and should be able to have them resolved.

chapters.summary: Lynch says providers are not pointing fingers but need better communication, clear responsibility, and genuine commitment. When there is a leak or no heat, someone must own the issue until resolved. She says older adults should not be caught in the middle of systems that do not communicate.
chapters.title: Lynch asks for better communication and clear responsibility

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: We are not here to point fingers or say that everything is wrong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: I know there are people within these agencies and management organizations who care and really want to help.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: We are asking for better communication, clear responsibility, and a genuine commitment to working together.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: When there is a leak, someone needs to own that issue until it is resolved.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: When there is no heat, there should be some urgency.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: When paperwork is preventing a capital project from moving forward, there needs to be a plan to get it done.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: We cannot continue to allow our older adults to be caught in the middle of systems that are not communicating with one another.

chapters.summary: Lynch says older adults have given much to their families and communities and should enjoy their centers without worrying about building conditions. She says aging in place requires caring for the places they depend on. She thanks the committee for the opportunity to speak.
chapters.title: Lynch concludes older adults deserve basics and peace of mind

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: Our older adults have already given so much of their families and communities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: They should be able to come to their center, sit with their friends, enjoy a meal, take part in activity, feel comfortable without worrying about the conditions of the building that they are in.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: They deserve that peace of mind.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: We also talk about aging in place, helping our older adults remain independent and improving their quality of life.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: We also need to make sure that the places they depend on are being cared for.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: Because at the end of the day, our older adults should not have to ask for the basics.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: They have earned the right to expect them.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Patricia Lynch
utterances.text: Thank you for listening and giving me the opportunity to speak today.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We just joined by Council Member Brewer.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We will now hear from our administration.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Oh, I forgot.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We will now hear testimony from administration.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We will now turn it to the community council, Amita.

chapters.summary: McKenzie introduces herself as Commissioner of the New York City Department for the Aging. She says there are 105 OACs primarily serving NYCHA residents across the five boroughs. She notes OACs provide more than 6.3 million meals and connect older adults to workforce, mental health, and elder justice services.
chapters.title: Commissioner Lisa Scott McKenzie introduces NYC Aging testimony and OAC portfolio

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Good morning, Chair Zwong, Chair Banks, and members of the New York City Council Committee on Aging and Committee on Public Housing.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I am Dr.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Lisa Scott McKenzie, Commissioner of the New York City Department for the Aging.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I appreciate the opportunity to testify before you today about older adult centers in New York City, housing authority facilities, and to speak on Introduction 1083.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Throughout the New York City Aging Portfolio of Programs, there are 105 OACs primarily serving NYCHA residents across the five boroughs.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: These represent a range of OAC types, including some of our largest and smallest centers.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: As we have discussed in past hearings, OACs are a critical component of the many services and programs offered to older New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: In addition to the important work of providing more than 6.3 million meals at OACs in partnership with the council, older adults also need to be connected to other critical programs which address their needs.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: These include workforce programs, mental health services, or elder justice and elder abuse services.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Nearly 150,000 older adults attended an NYC Aging OAC throughout New York City in FY 2026.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Around one-third of those are NYCHA Center attendees.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Because of that fact, we are constantly

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: working to ensure that the services in these centers are efficient and meet the needs of older NYCHA residents.

chapters.summary: McKenzie says NYC Aging understands unique repair challenges in NYCHA buildings and works with NYCHA to address complaints. She is joined by NYCHA COO Eva Trimble. The Bureau of Community Services oversees 300-plus OAC and NORC programs and works closely with NYCHA.
chapters.title: McKenzie describes NYC Aging's work with NYCHA on repairs

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: As with NYCHA facilities themselves, we understand the unique challenges of repairs and maintenance in these buildings and work with our partners at NYCHA to address complaints when they are filed and rectify any pressing concerns when they may arise.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I just wanted to briefly mention the photos and thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I know it has become part of the tradition, but I'd really like to believe that there are fewer new photos because older issues are being resolved.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I am joined today by Eva Tremble, NYCHA Chief Operating Officer, who we work with closely at New York City Aging to address repair and facility needs at the many OACs within NYCHA complexes.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: The NYC Aging Bureau of Community Services oversees the 300-plus OAC and NORC programs in the five boroughs, and they work closely with NYCHA and their team to ensure that OACs are functional and problem-

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: or repairs are addressed quickly.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: That working relationship is pivotal to the success of NYCHA OAC locations and how we ensure that we deliver the best services for older New Yorkers possible.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Additionally, NYCHA has been part of the cabinet for older New Yorkers since the inaugural meeting in September 2022,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: and their partnership has led to a number of improvements in programming at these spaces, such as intergenerational initiatives, public safety, and transportation-related enhancements.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Like many partner agencies in government, NYCHA and NYC Aging work every day to better serve New Yorkers over 60 in our OACs, but also in ways beyond serving meals and programming at centers.

chapters.summary: McKenzie says NYC Aging has managed OACs in NYCHA facilities since the agency's founding. The first OAC in the nation, William Hodson Older Adult Center, is at Daniel Webster Houses. Additional OACs came from NYCHA to NYC Aging during the Bloomberg administration and again in 2018-2019, with no centers closed.
chapters.title: McKenzie recounts history of OACs in NYCHA facilities

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: NYC Aging has managed OACs located at NYCHA facilities since the founding of our agency and the establishment of centers through the Older Americans Act.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: As you know, the nation's first OAC, William Hodson Older Adult Center in the Bronx, is located at Daniel Webster Houses and serves the older adult population in that complex as well as the surrounding community.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: While NYC Aging always has had some OACs in NYCHA sites, newly added OACs came from NYCHA to NYC Aging in two distinct tranches.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: First, during the Bloomberg administration, NYC Aging took on a number of centers, which NYCHA was no longer able to run independently and fold.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: those into our current network based on a range of factors, including size, space, and capacity, as well as budgetary needs for our agency.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Then in 2018 through 2019, NYC Aging assumed oversight over all remaining older adult centers still managed by NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: A similar situation occurred with other NYCHA social programs for children, where the Department of Youth and Community Development took on new programs as well.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: It is noteworthy that during these transitions from NYCHA to NYC Aging, not one center was closed.

chapters.summary: McKenzie says OACs report issues to NYCHA's Customer Contact Center and receive a ticket number. NYCHA addresses issues through property management or vendors based on complexity. Major issues like roof leaks or flooding are triaged differently based on severity.
chapters.title: McKenzie explains formal repair reporting system with NYCHA

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: In order to provide older adults at OACs a safe experience, we have a formal system in place with our partners at NYCHA to report and address issues or complaints when they arise.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: First, the center itself should report an issue to NYCHA by calling the Customer Contact Center.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: NYCHA-located OACs maintain the relationship with property managers for facility repairs like any other center would with any other landlord.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: For center issues reported to NYCHA's CCC, NYCHA will issue a ticket number to the individual who reported the problem,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: and the issue is either addressed by property management or by a NYCHA vendor based on complexity.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Major issues such as roof and ceiling leaks or flooded spaces will still receive a ticket number, but will be triaged differently based on the severity and impact to the space,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: OAC, or older adults themselves.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: In all cases, NYC Aging prioritizes service, continuity, and safety, and we do everything we can to ensure that centers remain open.

chapters.summary: McKenzie says NYC Aging and NYCHA liaison Agnes Mack reviews open tickets and needs at individual centers. If a ticket remains open, a second inquiry or visit to the property manager escalates the complaint. NYC Aging can raise issues to NYCHA's Office of Public-Private Partnerships.
chapters.title: McKenzie describes liaison and escalation process for open tickets

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: To better monitor these repairs and determine which need to be escalated, the NYC Aging

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: and NITRA liaison, Agnes Mack, who is a senior director of community services, regularly reviews reports of open tickets and needs at individual centers.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Our goal is to create constant communication and open dialogue between our agencies to ensure that repairs do not languish

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: and needs are addressed quickly.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: During repairs, if a center is closed for whatever reason, older adults at those locations will clearly know that they have other options for meals and programming at nearby centers or any other alternatives that best meet their needs.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: When a repair ticket remains open, a second inquiry is made or a visit to the property manager takes place to escalate the complaint.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: NYC Aging is then notified of a repeat issue and has the option to raise the issue to the NYCHA's Office of Public-Private Partnerships, where we regularly address issues with NYCHA facility staff and work toward a quick resolution for that center.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Because we are in NYCHA space, while NYC Aging may wish to fix an issue ourselves, we are not always able to do so and must rely on NYCHA to escalate it.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: the matter further in order to remedy the situation.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We do much of that escalation through the NYCHA liaison at NYC Aging, who manages the process for meeting with NYCHA and ensuring that we appropriately escalate matters in order to avoid center closures or alterations to programming.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: It is imperative that we monitor and respond quickly to repair issues so that there is no disruption to services for older adults.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Ultimately, this is really about the working relationship between NYCHA and NYC Aging.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: The size of the portfolio within NYCHA spaces is too large to ignore the great need that older New Yorkers have in these spaces and experience on a daily basis.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And it is incumbent upon us to ensure that we maintain a productive working relationship between NYC Aging and NYCHA.

chapters.summary: McKenzie says NYC Aging completed 56 projects across the OAC portfolio in FY26, many made possible by a $5 million council grant. Collaborations with NYCHA included a kitchen renovation at Bronx River OAC and roof and AC replacement at Samuel Tilden OAC. She says these improvements are impactful.
chapters.title: McKenzie reports 56 completed OAC projects and NYCHA collaborations

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We are happy to report that in FY26, NYC Aging has completed 56 projects across the OAC portfolio, and many of those were made possible because of the $5 million council

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: grant that has been included in the FY26 budget.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We also did complete collaborations with NYCHA Spaces for a kitchen renovation at Bronx River OAC and a roof and AC replacement at Samuel Tilden OAC.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: These improvements are impactful for older adults and we are grateful for our partnership with NYCHA as we address these concerns.

chapters.summary: McKenzie says federal investment in NYCHA facilities is needed as the older adult population grows. About one-third of the OAC portfolio is in NYCHA facilities. NYCHA and NYC Aging teams have committed to meeting quarterly to address persistent and acute issues.
chapters.title: McKenzie calls for federal investment and quarterly NYCHA meetings

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: As I know council is aware, overarching throughout the discussion,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: discussion today is the need for federal investment in NYCHA facilities.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: New York's older adult population continues to grow and as I've said before in today's testimony roughly one-third of our overall OAC portfolio is located in a NYCHA facility.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Because of that need, NYCHA and NYC Aging Teams have committed to meeting quarterly

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: to address persistent and acute issues affecting this portfolio of OACs.

chapters.summary: McKenzie says NYCHA pursues RAD through PACT programs. When a development converts, OACs remain with licensing agreements between them and the new landlord. The agreement outlines space needs and interaction between provider and landlord. NYC Aging approaches transitions on a site-by-site basis.
chapters.title: McKenzie explains RAD/PACT conversions and OAC licensing agreements

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Additionally, NYCHA has pursued the Rental Assistance Demonstration, RAD, through their Permanent Affordability Commitment Together programs, PACT.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: NYC Aging has needed to work more closely with NYCHA as the relationship with our centers has evolved or changed with these programs.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: When a NYCHA development converts through their program, OACs remain at those locations with licensing agreements between them and the new landlord once NYCHA has relinquished control of the site.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: This agreement also outlines the space needs for that location and the interaction between the provider and landlord.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: As the PAC program continues to develop through NYCHA, more OACs are being involved in those changes and approach these transitions on a site-by-site basis.

chapters.summary: McKenzie says NYC Aging takes seriously NYCHA's relationship with resident association presidents. OACs are required to maintain advisory councils of older adult participants who hear complaints and suggestions. NYC Aging recently convened the first-ever meeting of NYCHA RA presidents to address longstanding issues.
chapters.title: McKenzie discusses resident association engagement and advisory councils

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Additionally, we take seriously NYCHA's relationship with the resident association presidents at NYCHA and their commitment to their...

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Developments in the community of residents who utilize common areas and shared spaces like OACs.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: NYC Aging OACs

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: are required to maintain advisory councils of older adult participants who host regular meetings and hear complaints or suggestions regarding how these centers are run and managed.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We recognize that there can be some inevitable overlap between the RA presidents, resident councils, and the advisory councils serving older adults in those locations.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: That is why we recently convened the first ever of NYCHA RA presidents at NYC Aging to begin working through these longstanding issues.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We plan to continue these meetings to ensure an open line of communication with our RA partners, who we value as fundamental to successfully running centers in NITRA spaces.

chapters.summary: McKenzie says Intro 1083 would require the Commissioner of Aging to designate at least one financial literacy advisor in each OAC for at least 20 hours a month. NYC Aging agrees with the intent to improve older adults' financial livelihood. The agency is reviewing concerns and looks forward to discussions.
chapters.title: McKenzie comments on Intro 1083 financial literacy advisors

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Additionally, I am here to speak on Introduction 1083, sponsored by Councilmember Crystal Hudson, regarding the designation of financial literacy advisors to serve in older adult centers.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: This bill would require the Commissioner of Aging to designate at least one financial literacy advisor to serve in each older adult center for at least 20 hours a month.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We agree with the shared intent to improve the personal or financial livelihood of older adults.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: That is fundamental to our work.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: As with any programmatic change, we are reviewing for any concerns with our agency partners, which may have an impact on our providers.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We look forward to ongoing discussions regarding how we can best support older adults in managing their financial and legal well-being.

chapters.summary: McKenzie says NYC Aging is pleased to serve nearly 150,000 older adults through OACs, including in NYCHA developments. She says NYC Aging and NYCHA have a strong relationship and will continue strengthening it. She turns the testimony over to NYCHA Chief Operating Officer Eva Trimble.
chapters.title: McKenzie concludes NYC Aging testimony and turns to NYCHA COO

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: At New York City Aging, we are pleased to provide services to

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: to the nearly 150,000 older adults served in FY 2026 through our OACs, including those within NYCHA developments.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And we look forward to continuing these efforts to address the needs of a growing population in New York City.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: NYC Aging and NYCHA have a very strong relationship, and we look forward to continuing to further strengthen the relationship for the benefit of older

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: NYCHA residents through our work in the Cabinet for Older New Yorkers and our daily interactions on facility needs and improvements to the overall network of older adult services.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I am grateful to Chair Zhuang and Chair Banks of the Aging and Public Housing Committees for your advocacy and continued partnership to support our older New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn things over to NYCHA Chief Operating Officer Eva Trimble, who will further...

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Who will speak further on NYCHA's relationship with OACs at their developments.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Eva Trimble introduces herself as NYCHA Chief Operating Officer. She says NYCHA campuses are home to 77 older adult centers, with an additional 28 at PACT developments. These sites offer recreational, health, community, and cultural programs for NYCHA residents and other seniors.
chapters.title: NYCHA COO Eva Trimble introduces NYCHA OAC portfolio

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Chairs Banks and Swang, members of the Committee of Public Housing and Committee of Aging, and other distinguished members of the City Council, NYCHA residents, community advocates, and members of the public.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I am Eva Trimble, Chief Operating Officer at NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Thank you to Commissioner Scott McKenzie for your testimony and partnership.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: And thank you to the council for this opportunity to discuss older adult centers at NYCHA developments across the city.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: NYCHA's campuses are home to 77 older adult centers, and there are additional 28 centers at PAC developments.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: These sites offer a range of recreational, health, and community services.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: cultural programs that enhance the lives of NYCHA residents and other seniors in the community.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: On any given day, seniors benefit from meals, exercise classes, discussion groups, counseling, social services, technology classes, blood pressure screenings, and much more.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Our belief is the power of partnership drives our efforts to transform our organization and how we deliver services to residents.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: And it also drove NYCHA's decision years ago to transfer the operation of most of our older adult centers to NYC Aging and other partners who provide programming.

chapters.summary: Trimble says NYCHA and service providers share responsibility for maintaining centers. NYCHA is generally responsible for building systems and coordinating repairs, while providers handle interior maintenance. The PACT program is a critical tool for comprehensive modernization of community centers and apartments.
chapters.title: Trimble explains shared maintenance responsibilities and PACT modernization

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: NYCHA and the service providers share responsibility for maintaining the centers.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: As the landlord, NYCHA is generally responsible for repairing building systems, coordinating with the service provider to complete those repairs, and the provider is generally responsible for all interior maintenance and repairs.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: The PAC program is one of our critical tools for NYCHA to drive comprehensive modernization and renovations to community centers in addition to renovating apartments.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Removing lead, mold, and completing other comprehensive building improvements, all while keeping the buildings and land publicly owned and maintaining key resident rights.

chapters.summary: Trimble says NYCHA joined the mayor and Edenwald Houses Resident Association to celebrate the reopening of Edenwald Senior Center after 25 years. NYCHA participates in the Cabinet for Older New Yorkers and connects seniors to services. The HUD-funded Elderly Safe at Home program offers on-site assistance, home visits, and workshops.
chapters.title: Trimble highlights Edenwald Senior Center reopening and elder services

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Last week, we joined the mayor and Edenwald Houses Resident Association and PAC partners to celebrate the reopening of the Edenwald Senior Center after being inoperable for 25 years.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: NYC Aging is just one of our many critical partners.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: NYCHA participates in the NYC C.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: for older New Yorkers, which convenes nearly 30 New York City agencies to help address the needs of aging adults.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We also connect NYCHA seniors to services right where they live.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: The HUD-funded Elderly Safe at Home program, for instance, offers on-site assistance at several NYCHA developments, supporting older adults through home visits, connections to services,

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: workshops, and help from floor captains, residents who volunteer to support their neighbors.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: At NYCHA, we support older adults as they age in place with grace and dignity in a variety of ways, from older adult center programming provided by our partners to the dedicated services at our senior-only buildings.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: New affordable housing for seniors developed on our campuses.

chapters.summary: Trimble says NYCHA is proud of its work supporting older adults aging in place with dignity. She says NYCHA is eager to do more in partnership with NYC Aging and the City Council. She offers to answer questions.
chapters.title: Trimble concludes NYCHA testimony and offers to answer questions

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We are very proud of this work, and we are always eager to do more in service to the community, especially in partnership with stakeholders like NYC Aging and the City Council.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Thank you for your support and for this opportunity to dialogue with you on this important topic.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I'm happy to answer any questions that you may have.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you for your testimony.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks how many seniors are served by the 105 NYCHA OACs. McKenzie answers that 12,686 older adults receiving NYC Aging services live in NYCHA across all programs, including OAC participants. Zhuang expresses surprise at the number.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks how many seniors are served by 105 NYCHA OACs

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And we do have, I'm going to ask some questions.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We just also joined by Council Member Ressler and Council Member Hudson.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And I'm going to ask some questions, and then I'm going to give to you the floor.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Aside from location, is there any...

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Location about nature allocated

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So from the testimony, I see there's 105 NITRA OACs located in NITRA buildings.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: How many senior we actually serve from that 105 OACs?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Sorry, there are 12,686 older adults that receive NYC Aging Services who we know live in NYCHA across all programs, including our OAC participants.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks what challenges OAC providers in NYCHA facilities report as unique. McKenzie says repair and maintenance issues are not unique because many old buildings have needs. She says NYC Aging has completed 88% of smaller "just do-it" repairs through quarterly meetings with NYCHA leadership.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about challenges unique to OACs in NYCHA facilities

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: What challenges have OAC providers in NYCHA facilities reported you are unique to those OACs?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I wouldn't say the issues are unique when it comes to repair and maintenance because we know throughout New York City there are many buildings that are very old and they have extensive maintenance and repair needs.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: But I would say that there were some, as many of you know, I've embarked on a tour, a provider tour of all of our sites, and I've visited quite a few of our OACs that are located in NYCHA facilities.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And I'd say there are many things that we've considered to be just do-its that are smaller, minor repairs that can be effectuated pretty quickly that also add significantly to the quality of life that our older adults experience.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So we've been able to complete 88% of those, and that's through the framework that we've developed with NYCHA, where we're sitting quarterly with NYCHA leadership, including the CEO, Lisa Bova-Hyatt,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: many of the leadership that are represented here today from NYCHA and from NYC Aging, where we're able to discuss the escalation of some of the tickets that we consider to be critical.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks what the process is if there is a leak in a senior OAC in a NYCHA building. Trimble says providers first file a work ticket through NYCHA's Customer Contact Center. NYCHA sends a maintenance worker to assess; roof or major pipe leaks are NYCHA's responsibility, while leaks inside the center are the provider's responsibility.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about process for a leak in a NYCHA OAC

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: If there's a leaking in senior OAC in NITRA building, what's the process?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So when a provider has a condition in their site, their first step is to put in a work ticket through our CCC, our Customer Contact Center, and then NYCHA will send out a maintenance worker to assess the condition.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: As I mentioned in my testimony,

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: External conditions such as the facade, roof, and major building systems are typically the responsibility of NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So if the leak is caused by a roof issue or major pipe issue, leak from above, which is very common in our buildings, then it will be NYCHA's responsibility to fix it.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: If it's a leak underneath the sink or something within the center, then it is the provider's responsibility to fix it.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So if the maintenance worker comes out and determines it's something that we will fix, then we will typically sequence it to our skill trades and start working on the repair.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks if Trimble is familiar with LaGuardia and Dyckman Older Adult Senior Center. She says she heard they have a second-floor pipe leak that has not been fixed for years, requiring a bucket when someone showers. Trimble says she can follow up and will check whether it is on their repair list.
chapters.title: Zhuang raises LaGuardia and Dyckman OAC leak complaints

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Do you familiar with LaGuardia and the Dyckman Older Adult Senior Center?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I'm familiar with those centers, but not any specific conditions there.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I heard they have leaking on their second floor.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: The pipe has leaking.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: They haven't able to fix there for years.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And if there's anyone shower second floor, they have to put a bucket there.
