utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I just don't know what's the process and what's the status in that location.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Sure, I can certainly follow up on that.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: That's at LaGuardia and Dyckman, the same condition?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Sure, we can follow up on that.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Because this is what complaint we usually hear, not only just them, but this is just come, they were there in previous testimony.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I also want to share that we, as the Commissioner Scott McKenzie mentioned, our staff meets every two weeks to review.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: repair requests and so we'll check whether that is on our list.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: If it hasn't been escalated, we will go and we'll take a look and see what those conditions are.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I hope I can hear from you very soon about these two locations leaking issue.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks who makes proposals and how NYCHA is looped in when opening a new OAC in NYCHA property. McKenzie says all centers are contracted through an RFP process, and NYC Aging has an OAC RFP scheduled for later this year. New sites would follow the same RFP and contract process.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about process for opening a new OAC in NYCHA property

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Can you describe the process for opening and operating OAC?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Located in NITCHER property.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Who make the proposal and to who?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And how the NITCHER looped in that process?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: What is the timeline for proposal to opening?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Are you referencing a new center, opening a new center?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Yes, new center.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Any center.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: If you open a new center, who you are proposed to?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Well, all of our centers are contracted, and that's usually in response to the RFP process.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: As you know, we have an OAC RFP that's scheduled to come out perhaps later this year that we're discussing.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: But for any new sites where we deem there may be the need for a new site, we would have to follow that same process, the RFP process, then a contract process.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So I'm assuming then that it would be NYC Aging.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks if there is a plan to expand the number of OACs within NYCHA facilities as the older adult population grows. McKenzie says NYC Aging has looked at where older adults reside and provided heat maps to council partners. The new RFP process will help identify needs and potential new centers, but nothing is determined yet.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about expanding OACs in NYCHA facilities

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And as the older adults population in New York City growing significantly, is there any plan for expanding the number of older adults center within NYCHA facility?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Well, we have looked at where our older adults are now residing.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Obviously, there's been a lot of change, and NYC Aging did provide heat maps to our council partners to advise them of where we've seen some of the migration of older adults.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And so obviously with this new RFP process, we will be able to look at where the needs are, who's interested in serving the increased population in those areas, and there could potentially be new.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: centers and OACs at NITRA facilities, but we don't know that yet.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks what metrics or evaluation processes assess the impact of OACs on older adults in NYCHA housing. McKenzie says NYC Aging uses several metrics reported in the Mayor's Management Report and other reports. She mentions surveys on food and programs and recent food town halls.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about metrics to assess OAC impact on older adults

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: What's the metric or evaluation process in the place to assess the impact of OACs on the overall well-being of older adults in NITRA housing?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: What metric or evaluation process are in place to assess the impact of OACs on the overall well-being of older adults in NITRA housing?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: In OACs and NYCHA housing, the well-being of older adults, we have, for NYC Aging, obviously there are several metrics that we use to look at the health and well-being of

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: our participants in our programs.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And, you know, obviously they're listed in the Mayor's Management Report.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We have several other reports in which we report our statistics on...

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: The services and programs that we provide and whether there's a wait list or case management, caregiver services, there's so many services.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So I'm not sure if there's anything specific you're looking for.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks what services NYC Aging provides in those locations. McKenzie says many services are provided. She elaborates on food surveys and town halls, noting older adults have given feedback on plant-based meals. Brooklyn's food town hall is scheduled for tomorrow.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about services provided in NYCHA OACs

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Any service you guys provide in those locations?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: In the OACs?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Many, many, many services.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Surveys, surveys.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: There are some surveys that we do conduct.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And again, I'm trying to get at the root of the specificity because obviously there's surveys pertaining to food and programs.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So I don't know if there's anything specific that you're looking for, but we'd be willing to share, obviously, what we've seen.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I'll talk a little bit about what we've done recently with the surveys for food, because obviously we've had a lot of feedback from older adults about some of the meals, and some of them are not as pleased right now, we know, with the plant-based meals and so on.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So we've been talking with them across the city.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: In fact, we've conducted food town halls in every borough so far except Brooklyn.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Brooklyn is tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: But we've received some really, really robust feedback.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: As we know, older adults are very vocal and they're not shy.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So they've shared their thoughts about our new recipes that we're proposing because at each one of these food town halls, we've also provided taste tests and samples for older adults to try.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And we've had some real-time surveys right at the site.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So we've been able to share with the older adults, too, what they've said about some of these meals.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So we like to, and I think many of you know, have a very collaborative stance when it comes to our older New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We like to.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: to get their feedback and to be able to provide them with services that not only meet but hopefully exceed their expectations.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So those are the types of surveys that NYC Aging conducts.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks if there are staff shortages or challenges retaining qualified staff at NYCHA-based OACs compared to other OACs. McKenzie says she has not heard specifics about staff not wanting to work in NYCHA facilities. She praises the mission-driven commitment of OAC staff.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about staff shortages at NYCHA OACs

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Are there any staff shortage or challenge for...

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Retain qualified staff at work at the centers based in NITRA facility compared to regular other OACs.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We haven't heard any specifics on staff at OACs that are in NITRA facilities not wanting to work there.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I've been pleasantly surprised by the commitment that I see across all of our OACs with the staff that work there.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: They're really mission-driven people that are passionate about the work of protecting older adults.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So I haven't heard any specific complaints.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks how many case managers are present at OACs in NYCHA facilities. McKenzie says she will have to get back with the number but says staffing is adequate at most centers. She has heard of one or two centers recruiting additional case managers.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks how many case managers are at NYCHA OACs

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, overall, how many case managers are present at OACs located in NICHE facilities?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I'll have to get back to you on the number of case managers, but we do have adequate staffing at most of them.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I have heard of maybe one or two where they are right now recruiting additional case managers, so we'd have to provide you more information.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks if case managers at NYCHA OACs receive specialized training for the unique experience of older adults in NYCHA housing. McKenzie says all case managers receive customized training based on the site and population served. That extends to NYCHA facilities.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about tailored training for case managers at NYCHA OACs

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Do case managers at NITCHA OACs receive specially or tailored training to prepare them for unique experience of older adults in NITCHA housing?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Well, all of our case managers receive customized.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: training based on the site that they will be assigned to, the population that they will be serving.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So that would extend to folks that are in NYCHA facilities as well.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks what the difference is between a case manager working in a NYCHA facility and one not working in a NYCHA facility. McKenzie says training is not based on the facility but on the population served and their unique needs. She says they do not base training on the facility type.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks difference between case managers in NYCHA vs non-NYCHA OACs

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: What's the difference between the case manager working in

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: NICHE facility and the case manager not working in NICHE facility?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Well, we don't base the training on the facility.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We base it on the population served and what would be the unique needs of the older adults in that particular area.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks about the administration's long-term vision for OACs in NYCHA property and how it aligns with supporting the aging population. McKenzie says there is a strong commitment to support older adults and help them live with dignity and respect. She says OACs should be welcoming, safe, and functional.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about long-term vision for OACs in NYCHA property

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: What is administration's long-term vision for OAC's nature property, and how does it align with broader effort to support NYC aging population?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Well, I know that there's a very strong commitment from the administration to support older adults, to make sure that they're living their best possible life here in New York City,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: and to provide the supports necessary for them to be able to thrive and live with dignity and respect.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So that's what we expect at each one of the older adult centers that we're operating, that our older adults find them welcoming places where they can come and really enjoy the services there in a safe, functional environment.

chapters.summary: Zhuang says McKenzie's answer is general and asks for a more detailed vision, such as more food pantries or caseworkers. McKenzie cites food pop-up produce events in August that distributed over 18,000 bags of fresh produce. She says NYC Aging plans to repeat this for the holiday period with 20 pop-up locations.
chapters.title: Zhuang presses for specific plans for food pantries and caseworkers

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Do you have any particular case, say, next year we're going to do more food pantry or caseworker in those facilities?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I feel your answer is very general.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Can we?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: have a better, like, detailed vision.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Well, I think I've been very clear about the vision for NYC Aging.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I know that many of you are aware of the food pop-up produce events that we held in August, which is in response, basically, to the fact that many of our older adults had issues with their SNAP benefits,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: and also that we received less than half of the farmer's market vouchers that we normally receive.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So that's how we responded in August, and we were able to distribute over 18,000 bags of fresh produce.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We're planning again now to do this for the holiday period because we recognize that this is another time of strain for older adults when they may want to share in family meals and have others over.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So from mid-November through the first two weeks of December, we're going to do this again.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And during August, we had 10 pop-up locations.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: This time we're going to go for 20 pop-up locations to make more locations available for older adults.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So, of course, making sure that we address those core elements in our revised mission, which is that we're combating food insecurity.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We're also providing access for affordable housing wherever we can, addressing health care and making sure that there's access to quality health care and ensuring that our older adults are safe.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks how many food bags NYC Aging provides to NYCHA facility senior OACs. McKenzie says they can break that out but did not for this meeting. She notes older adults can pick up food bags at any site regardless of where they live.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks how many food bags go to NYCHA OACs

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Do you have, how many food bags do you provide the NITCHER facility senior OAs?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We can break that out for you.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I didn't break it out for this meeting, but we can break that out.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: But obviously, because someone lives in NITRA doesn't mean that they have to pick up a food bag in NITRA.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: They can go wherever they want.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So as long as they are 60 or older, regardless of income, immigration status, or residency where they live, they can go to any one of those sites and receive the same treatment as anyone else.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And then let me turn the floor to Coach here.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thanks.

chapters.summary: Banks asks if any OACs on NYCHA property are considered common areas or commercial spaces. Trimble says they are not commercial spaces; they are community spaces. Banks confirms they are community spaces.
chapters.title: Banks asks if OACs on NYCHA property are common or commercial spaces

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And again, thank you for your testimony.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Specifically on the OAC infrastructure complaints and agency, obviously, your responses, we appreciate you to be concise with your response.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Are there any OACs on NITRA's property considered common areas or commercial spaces?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: No, they are not considered commercial spaces.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: They are community spaces.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: They're community spaces.

chapters.summary: Banks asks if OAC providers are considered tenants. McKenzie says OAC providers are not tenants. Banks notes there is no agreement between them.
chapters.title: Banks asks whether OAC providers are tenants

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Are the OAC providers considered tenants?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: OAC providers are not tenants.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So they're not tenants of the, okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So there's no agreement between them.

chapters.summary: Banks asks about dual-use community centers with youth on one side and seniors on the other. He asks if there is any internal framework or agreement between the agencies or entities occupying the center. Trimble says they can check specific co-location sites, but generally there are some license agreements for OACs and mostly no leases.
chapters.title: Banks asks about framework for co-located youth and senior centers

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So if it's a co-located dual youth center,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Like, you know, now you have centers that are now dual use.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You have the youth on one side and you have the seniors on the other side.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Is there any framework or agreement internally between the two agencies or entities that are occupying the community center?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We can double check any specific sites that may have co-locations, but in general, we have some license agreements in place for older adult centers.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: For the most part, we don't have any leases.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So it's very much on a case-by-case basis, depending on the conditions of the site that might have warranted a license agreement at some point.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So those license agreements are with the actual...

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We have just a handful of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Banks asks about the specific status of OACs and providers and how it affects NYCHA's work with them. Trimble says NYCHA works closely with NYC Aging and providers to coordinate repair and programming issues. Staff meet regularly, and information is shared through multiple channels.
chapters.title: Banks asks about OAC provider status and NYCHA coordination

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What is the specific status of the OACs and the OAC providers, and how does this affect the way NYCHA works with the OACs on their property?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So as we've been explaining, we work very closely in coordination with NYC Aging, as well as the providers, to coordinate any type of repair issues or certain programming issues.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Our staff meet regularly with NYC Aging, and with the providers, they speak to NYC Aging as well as they are contracted by NYC Aging.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So there are multiple ways that information is shared.

chapters.summary: Banks asks if there have been scenarios where NYCHA or DFTA had to mediate a controversy between a youth provider and an aging provider. McKenzie says she is not aware of any instances. She says the sibling agencies have good relationships and open communication.
chapters.title: Banks asks if NYCHA or DFTA mediated youth-provider disputes

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Has there been any scenarios or situations where...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: NICHA or DFTA had to mediate a relationship or any controversy that may have come up between the youth provider and the aging provider or the older adult provider?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I'm not aware of any instances.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I'd say that our sibling agency, we have very good relationships and collaboration.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So if there is an issue where we need to be able to talk to one another, that line of communication is very open.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We would be able to work it out.

chapters.summary: Banks asks specifically about responsibilities. McKenzie says it depends on the site, and a handful have different agreements. She says providers are clear that minor repairs inside the site are their responsibility.
chapters.title: Banks asks about repair responsibilities at co-located sites

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And specifically on responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Well, it depends on the site.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: As Ms.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Tremble mentioned a moment ago, there's a handful of sites that do have different agreements.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: But when it comes to responsibility for any issues that occur inside the site, our providers are very clear as to that it is their responsibility for minor repairs within the site.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how many facility-related complaints were filed by OACs in NYCHA buildings over the past year and how many were resolved. Trimble says approximately 1,700 work orders were submitted by older adult centers. Almost all were closed and completed by NYCHA, with about 250 still open, some pending responsibility determination.
chapters.title: Banks asks how many facility complaints were filed and resolved

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay, so then how many facility-related complaints were filed by OACs in NITRA buildings over the past year, and how many of these such complaints were resolved by DFTA or by NITRA?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Thank you, Councilmember.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Over the past year, we've had approximately 1,700 work orders submitted by older adult centers.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Almost all of those were closed and completed by NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We have about 250 that are still open right now.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: of those that are still open may still be in the process of determining responsibility between NYCHA and the provider.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: NYC Asian doesn't do any direct repairs themselves outside of their commitment with the funding they received from the council last year, but even that is transferred to their providers.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So it's really about meeting with the provider and determining whose responsibility the repair is.

chapters.summary: Banks asks if the 1,700 repair tickets are differentiated between the aging side and the youth center side in dual-use centers. Trimble says she is not familiar with how many co-location sites exist. She confirms the 1,700 number is specifically from older adult centers.
chapters.title: Banks asks if 1,700 tickets distinguish OAC vs youth center

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And of the 1,700 tickets that were put in or repair tickets,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Is it differentiated between what's on the center, the aging side or the older adults center side or the youth center side?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Or is it just for that particular center?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: When it's a dual youth center.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm not that familiar with how many sites we have that actually have those co-locations.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So the number, the 1700.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Well, if we can get that number.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We can definitely follow up with you on that number.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: The 1700 I'm quoting is specifically from older adult centers.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So this is specific, okay.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So that 1,700 is just complete.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Just on the older adult center side.

chapters.summary: Banks asks if there is a breakdown of the facilities for the outstanding 250 tickets. Trimble says they can send that information. Banks moves on to ask about DFTA evaluating infrastructure concerns.
chapters.title: Banks asks for breakdown of outstanding 250 tickets

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How many of the outstanding complaints are, well, you already gave that already.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Do we have a breakdown of the facilities of those outstanding 250 tickets?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We can send that to you.

chapters.summary: Banks asks if DFTA evaluates infrastructure concerns at NYCHA and coordinates with NYCHA. Trimble says staff meet every two weeks to review open repair requests using a shared tracker. Most repairs come through the CCC; NYCHA assesses and determines responsibility.
chapters.title: Banks asks how DFTA coordinates with NYCHA on infrastructure concerns

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Is DIFTA evaluating the infrastructure concerns to NITRA and coordinating with NITRA on these issues?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And what does that coordination look like?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I can start if you want.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So we, as I said, we meet regularly to go through open repair requests.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Our staff meet every two weeks.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We have a shared tracker that we're using to follow up on certain repair requests.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: They said most of the repairs come in through our CCC.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We'll send a maintenance worker to assess.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We'll determine whether we think it's our responsibility or the provider.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: If it goes back to the provider, they may reach out to aging for help or escalation.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: That may come back to us, and we can take another look.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: But for the most part, if it's anything that is a major system improvement or something from the building envelope, like I said, the roof or the facade or a major piping, then NYCHA will take care of it.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Banks asks OAC staff to describe the process for reporting a facility or maintenance issue in a NYCHA facility. Trimble says they call the CCC, NYCHA sends a maintenance worker, assesses the condition, and determines next steps. Banks notes NYCHA has said staff can escalate to the neighborhood administrator if a ticket stays open.
chapters.title: Banks asks process for OAC staff to report maintenance issues

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And can you please describe the process that the OAC staff must go through to report a facility or a maintenance issue in a NYCHA facility?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So they call the CCC, we'll send out a maintenance worker, we'll assess the condition and determine the next steps.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: We were also joined by Councilor Jose.

chapters.summary: Banks asks about average response time for maintenance and repair requests at OACs and how they are prioritized. Trimble says the average response time is about 12 days. Repairs face similar prioritization as residential units, with leaks and flooding highest and life-health-safety conditions prioritized.
chapters.title: Banks asks average response time and prioritization for OAC repairs

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: NITRA has stated that the OAC staff report repairs through the CCC and may escalate to the neighborhood administrator if the ticket stays open past the scheduled date.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What is the average response time for maintenance and repair requests at these OACs and how are they prioritized?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Our average response time is about 12 days, and they face similar prioritization as our residential units.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So leaks from above, any type of flooding conditions are always some of the highest.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Anything that's a life health safety condition, things that are lower priority tend to be things like door hinges or something that's just not life health safety related.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And we will also join my council on one.

chapters.summary: Banks asks about the public housing liaison role since 2021, who the liaison is, how many staff support them, and how often they engage with DFTA and NYCHA. McKenzie says a senior director serves as NYCHA liaison with two or three support staff. The liaison meets biweekly with NYCHA, and senior leadership meets quarterly.
chapters.title: Banks asks about public housing liaison role and staffing

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Since 2021, the designated liaisons have handled the OAC complaints.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Can you please describe the role of the public housing liaison in this process?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Who is the public housing liaison?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How many staff support this liaison?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And what offices does the liaison regularly engage with within DFTA and NYCHA and how often?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Well, on the DFTA side, we have a senior director assigned to the role of liaison for NYCHA, and there are approximately two or three people that support that role

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: along with the senior director.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: That senior director now is also joined by many members of leadership at DFTA because we do have those two meetings now.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: One that is a senior leader meeting along with the senior leadership at NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And then that secondary meeting that takes place every two weeks with the liaison between NYCHA and our senior director.

chapters.summary: Banks asks what determines whether a NYCHA facility-related complaint is logged into the Older Adult Center Metrics Report under Local Law 140 of 2018. McKenzie says any safety concern or anything that disrupts operations would be reported. She says 88% of "just do-it" complaints have been addressed, but some tickets remain open.
chapters.title: Banks asks about Local Law 140 logging of NYCHA complaints

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What determines whether NYCHA facility related complaints is logged into the older adult metrics report as required by local law 140 of 2018?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I'm sorry, would you repeat that question?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What determines whether a NITRA facility-related complaint is logged into the Older Adult Center Matrix Report as required by Local Law 40 of 2018?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Well, for us at DFTA, it would be any safety concern.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Anything that's going to disrupt operations would be reported.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Are there any outstanding complaints logged or any resolved complaints or issues that you're aware of?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Well, there are 88% of the complaints that we receive that we consider to be just do-its that need to be addressed immediately have been.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Of those, the...

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: There are some of the issues that Ms.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Trimble mentioned earlier.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: There are some outstanding tickets that are still open, and we're working together to get those resolved as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

chapters.summary: Banks says OAC staff spend hours navigating facility requests and are unsure which agency is responsible. Some report DFTA and NYCHA engage in finger-pointing. He asks which agency handles which infrastructure and repair requests and how they work together.
chapters.title: Banks raises provider reports of finger-pointing between DFTA and NYCHA

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: The OAC staff have reported that they sometimes can spend hours navigating facility requests.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And are often unsure of which agency is responsible for handling a particular facility issue.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Other staff have reported that DFTA and NITRA engage in finger-pointing, seeking to assign responsibility for repair requests to other agencies.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Please explain to us which facility.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Infrastructure and repair requests are handled

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: by and which agency and how the agencies work together to determine where responsibilities lies for each issue of OAC report.

chapters.summary: Trimble says she is troubled to hear providers report finger-pointing and says the relationship with NYC Aging has never been stronger. Staff meet every two weeks with a shared tracker and make site visits. McKenzie says providers are pleased with open, collaborative talks and know they can lean on NYC Aging.
chapters.title: Trimble and McKenzie dispute finger-pointing, describe coordination

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I'm definitely troubled to hear that you're hearing that from providers.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I can commit that our relationship with NYC Aging has never been stronger.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Our staff meet every two weeks to review a shared tracker of repair requests.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We've both been making site visits to centers.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: There's never been better communication, so we work hard to make sure providers know where to go to find answers, to make sure that those repairs are logged.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: As you know, with our residential repairs, sometimes it can take a while to complete the repair, but there should be no question as to whose ball the court is in.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So can you give us a break?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: In general, NYCHA does work that is related to the building systems, and the providers are responsible for all work inside the center.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And we do provide additional support for the providers as well.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I meet with them on a monthly basis.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: In addition to our tour where we're out in the site with our providers asking questions about the maintenance or any issues that we pick up while we're there.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So from what I've heard thus far from our providers, they're very pleased with having these very open, collaborative.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Talks and they know they can lean on us if they

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I do need any additional supports, and I think we have an excellent framework together with NYCHA now to be able to address anything that is considered a concern.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So I'm surprised to hear it as well.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: All right.

chapters.summary: Banks asks for clarity on what requests are handled by DFTA. McKenzie says DFTA handles minor repairs inside the unit, not capital needs or building systems. She gives examples like a broken doorknob or painting a wall.
chapters.title: Banks asks what repair requests DFTA handles

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Well, what requests are handled by DFTA?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I just want some clarity on that because I didn't get it.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Anything that would be considered inside the unit and a minor repair.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We don't handle anything that's a capital need.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We don't handle anything that has to do with the building system.

chapters.summary: Banks asks whether HVAC, ceiling holes, floor tiles, and bathrooms are NYCHA responsibilities. McKenzie says HVAC is absolutely NYCHA, ceiling holes depend on extent, floor tiles may be asbestos and go to NYCHA, and bathroom repairs depend on whether it is a plumbing system issue or minor repair. She says she uses her facilities management experience to decide.
chapters.title: Banks asks examples: HVAC, ceiling holes, floor tiles, bathrooms

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Can you give me an example?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: A broken doorknob.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: A broken doorknob, okay.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Something like that.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Or something, maybe a wall that someone wants to have painted, but very, very minor repairs.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And an HVAC system would be nitrous?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: A hole in the ceiling, it would be nitrous?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: More than likely, depending on what the hole is due to.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: You know, sometimes there are some minor, if it's one ceiling tile, we might prefer to do something like that ourselves.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: If it's an entire ceiling, you know, obviously that would be nitrous.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Tiles on the floor, nitrous or different?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Depends on the amount and also what it contains.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Many floor tiles could be asbestos.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: If it's asbestos, obviously we don't want to touch it.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: That would be something larger that NITRA would handle.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I should also mention, you know, I spent several years in facilities management myself.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So some of these things, as I'm walking through these sites, I can tell if it's something that, you know, we can handle this or if it's something that we cannot handle, and then we know to call in NITRA to get it.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: of that assistance and support.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And what about bathrooms?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: It depends on if it's a toilet that's leaking, something that might be a system of plumbing repair that would go to NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: If it's just repairing the bulb inside the bowl, we might decide to take on something like that.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: It's very small.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: You could go to Home Depot and fix that within a half an hour.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Something like that we would handle.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Something larger would go to NYCHA.

chapters.summary: Banks asks if McKenzie is aware of a leak issue at LaGuardia that has been ongoing for two years. McKenzie says they need to check outstanding tickets and notes she recently visited Dyckman and saw no leak there. She says they will look at LaGuardia and get back to him.
chapters.title: Banks asks about two-year leak at LaGuardia OAC

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So are you aware of the leak issue that has been taking place for two years at LaGuardia?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We have to go back and take a look at what tickets are still outstanding, but I can tell you I have personally been to Dykeman recently, and there was no evidence of a leak there while I was there.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So, again, we need to take a look at some of the issues, and perhaps you're hearing of something that happened in the past that might have been resolved, so we need to confirm that for you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So you're saying that the leaking issue at LaGuardia has been taken care of?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I didn't mention LaGuardia at all.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I said Dykeman.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: That was my question.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Well, my answer was that I've been to Dykeman and that we would take a look at LaGuardia and get back to you on it.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Well, we know that based off of reports that there's been an ongoing leak issue for the last two years, and hopefully we can get some resolution for that.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: It would be our pleasure to resolve something, especially if it's been going on for two years.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I think everyone is aware of how passionate I am about our...

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: older adults having safe, functional spaces that are also welcoming to them.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So if there's a leak going on for two years, definitely that's something we want to look at immediately.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you for that.

chapters.summary: Banks asks what instructions DFTA and NYCHA provide to OAC staff about which repairs each agency handles. McKenzie says they meet regularly and review open tickets to determine whether NYCHA or DFTA should handle an issue. She mentions 56 completed projects and says some open tickets may have been resolved by capital improvements.
chapters.title: Banks asks what instructions DFTA and NYCHA give OAC staff on repairs

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What instructions does DFTA and NYCHA provide to the OAC staff on which kinds of repairs or facility requests are handled by each respective agency?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Well, as I mentioned earlier, we do meet quite regularly and we look at the open tickets.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And as we're looking at those open tickets, we can determine whether there's something that, again, NYCHA would have to take on or if there's something that in looking at the list, it's so minor that DFTA might be able to take a look at it and see what we can do.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I also want to mention and go back to my previous testimony about the 56 projects that we just completed.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So our last meeting a couple weeks ago was that we wanted to take a look at some of those open tickets and determine whether or not some of them have also been resolved by these major capital improvements that we've made over the last year.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So there may be a further reduction on those tickets that are outstanding.

chapters.summary: Banks asks for the list of 56 projects and congratulates NYC Aging on the progress. McKenzie thanks the council for the investment and says they have made good use of the money. Banks says more work remains.
chapters.title: Banks requests list of 56 completed projects

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Yeah, if you could provide the list of the 56 projects, you know, we always welcome any progress.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And congratulations on that.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: More work to be done.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And thank you so much for the investment from the council.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: As you can see, we've made good use of the money.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Excellent, excellent, excellent.

chapters.summary: Banks asks if DFTA has a formalized process for following up with NYCHA to ensure repairs are resolved. McKenzie says yes, through the same framework. If an issue is not resolved by the two-week or one-month mark, they develop a corrective action plan.
chapters.title: Banks asks about formal follow-up process when repairs go to NYCHA

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: When a repair or facility request is passed on to NYCHA,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Does DFTA have a formalized process for following up with NITRA to ensure that the issue is resolved?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Through the same framework that we talked about, if the issue is not resolved by the two-week mark or the one-month mark where we are all sitting together, then obviously we need to come up with a corrective action plan that addresses it.

chapters.summary: Banks asks if that process would prevent a situation like a leak going on for two years. McKenzie says it should, and if not, they need to find the gap or deficiency. Banks says a two-year situation means the system is not working.
chapters.title: Banks asks if follow-up would prevent two-year leak

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And that would prevent a situation like a leaky situation going on for two years, right?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: It should.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And if it has not prevented that, then we need to look at where there's a gap or a deficiency that needs to be corrected.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So if there's obviously a situation that has been going on for two years, that means obviously the system is not working.

chapters.summary: Trimble says they need to look at the specific condition at LaGuardia. She says it is possible NYCHA repaired a leak and it returned because plumbing systems are old and outdated. She says it may be a symptom of ongoing infrastructure problems, not a failure to respond.
chapters.title: Trimble says recurring leaks may reflect old infrastructure

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Well, we have to take a look at what that condition actually is.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So I also want to be clear, it's possible that we repaired a leak at LaGuardia.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: As you know, our leaks come back, right?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: These are the original plumbing systems in our buildings, which are extremely old and outdated.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So it's possible that we've repaired the leak and it keeps returning over the course of the two years.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So it's not that the system isn't working or that we're not responding.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: It could just be a symptom of the ongoing problems with our infrastructure.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So I think we have to take a look at the specific incident and see what's going on.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Banks asks what the liaison's role is in the repair process. McKenzie says the liaison is critical and sits in the biweekly meeting with the NYCHA liaison. They go ticket by ticket to ensure resolution or explain why tickets remain outstanding. Reports go to senior leadership quarterly.
chapters.title: Banks asks about liaison's role in repair process

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What is the liaison's role in this process?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: The liaison is critical.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: They sit in that meeting, the biweekly meeting, along with the liaison on the NITRA side, and they leave.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: literally go ticket by ticket to ensure that those tickets have been either resolved or if they're outstanding, they can give us specifics as to why it's still outstanding.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And the report that they give us after their two meetings is reviewed by the senior leadership when we meet regularly on a quarterly basis.

chapters.summary: Banks asks if the division of responsibility is written anywhere. McKenzie says there are functional job descriptions for the liaison and the council mandated the liaison role. She says they use that framework to meet the needs of older New Yorkers.
chapters.title: Banks asks if division of responsibility is written anywhere

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And is this division of responsibility written anywhere?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We do have, obviously, functional job descriptions for the liaison.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I know that the council also has mandated that there is this liaison.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So, yes, we're using all of that framework to ensure that the work meets the needs of our older New Yorkers.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Yeah.

chapters.summary: Banks asks if there is an agreement between NYCHA and DFTA on the responsibility of the liaison. McKenzie says the current framework is better than waiting for an MOU. She says they meet quarterly, liaisons meet, and tickets are reviewed regularly.
chapters.title: Banks asks if there is an agreement between NYCHA and DFTA on liaison

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Is there an agreement between NITRA and DIFTA on the responsibility of the liaison?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: In my opinion, the framework that we have now is even greater than having an MOU or waiting for an MOU process.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I think what we've done immediately is to start to hit the ground running with making sure that we agree that we're going to meet quarterly, that we do have the framework for our liaisons to meet,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: and that we are reviewing tickets regularly and also resolving issues right away.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So, no, I think the written agreement couldn't be better than what we have right now.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Banks notes NYCHA has said it does not have a repair agreement similar to its DYCD agreement. He asks if that is still accurate. Trimble says yes, that is accurate. Banks asks if NYCHA has sent a proposed agreement to DFTA.
chapters.title: Banks asks if NYCHA has a repair agreement with DFTA

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: NITRA has stated in the past that it does not have a repair agreement, and I think we touched on that agreement with DFTA.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: But once similar to what it has with the DYCD agreement, is that still accurate?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Yes, that's accurate.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Does NITRA have a repair agreement with DFTA?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We do not.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You know?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Banks asks if NYCHA has sent a proposed agreement to DFTA and if there is a plan to do so. Trimble says it is an ongoing conversation, but in the meantime they are doing what they would do under an agreement. Staff meet biweekly and leadership meets quarterly.
chapters.title: Trimble says agreement with DFTA is ongoing conversation

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And has NITRA sent a proposed agreement to DFTA?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And if so, is there a plan to send an agreement to DFTA?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: It's an ongoing conversation, but as Commissioner mentioned, in the meantime, we are doing all of the things.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: that we would do under such agreement anyway.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Our staff are meeting biweekly between the liaison and my staff in operations.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We're going through all the repair requests, and leadership is meeting on a quarterly basis to review that work.

chapters.summary: Banks asks what main hurdles prevent outstanding complaints from being resolved. Trimble says it depends on the nature of the complaint. Significant leaks may require tracing or larger plumbing initiatives, and plastering work has significant delays, potentially six months.
chapters.title: Banks asks about hurdles preventing complaint resolution

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: If a complaint is outstanding, what are the main hurdles or challenges that prevent the complaint from being resolved?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: It depends on the nature of the complaint.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Again, similar to our conditions across our buildings, if it's a significant leak problem, it may be that we are tracing the leak, that we are working on a larger plumbing initiative.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: It really depends on the specific issue.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: As you know, we have a significant delay specifically to our plastering work.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So if the complaint is about plastering, they could be waiting six months or so for a plaster to come and make that repair.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: We will also join by Councilmember Dineritz.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Banks asks if NYCHA tracks OAC tickets separately from apartment or common space repair tickets. Trimble says yes, they are marked to the OAC. Banks asks about average time to resolve OAC complaints.
chapters.title: Banks asks if NYCHA tracks OAC tickets separately

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Does NYCHA track the OAC tickets separately from the apartments or the common space area repair tickets?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Yes, they are marked to the OAC.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: To the OAC, okay.

chapters.summary: Banks asks the average time from complaint to resolution at NYCHA OACs. Trimble says average days to close a work order at OACs is 12.8 days. She says information is tracked in NYCHA's internal Maximo system, and providers can look up open tickets on NYCHA's service page.
chapters.title: Banks asks average time to resolve OAC complaints and portal access

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And what is the average amount of time from when a complaint is filed to when a complaint is resolved across the OAC?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: OACs at a NITRA facility.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Our average days to close a work order at OACs is 12.8 days.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And is this information tracked perhaps in any online portal and where requests can be logged in or monitored?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: All of that information is tracked in our internal asset management system, our Maximo system, just like our work tickets for the residential units.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So an OAC provider is not able to see or track the...

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: They should be able to look up their open work tickets on our service page on our website.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how many OACs were closed for repairs in the past year. Trimble says three centers were closed due to unsafe conditions: Glebe Avenue, Latimer Gardens, and Randall Avenue/Balcombe. Banks asks about remediation updates.
chapters.title: Banks asks how many OACs closed for repairs in past year

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Does Nitro Diff to track how many overseas closed repairs in the past year?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Sorry, closed for repairs in the last year.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Oh, closed for repairs, yes.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Right now there are three centers that have been closed in the past year due to unsafe conditions.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Gleebe Avenue, Latimer Gardens, and Randall Avenue, Balcombe.

chapters.summary: Banks asks about remediation at centers, mentioning Cypress Houses and possible mold or asbestos remediation. Trimble says NYCHA is working on lead abatement at daycare centers. She says priority is to maintain center operations during repairs, but life-health-safety issues like asbestos or lead may require closure and relocation.
chapters.title: Banks asks about remediation and possible closures at Cypress Houses

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I know recently there's been some remediation that's been done to some of the centers,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: which has caused some of them operations to be moved or closed to some degree.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Is there any update on the amount of centers that have received a remediation?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We are currently working on lead abatement at our daycare centers.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: And I don't know if that's what you're referring to when you say remediation.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Well, I know there was a, I know at Cypress Houses, I know there was a concern, and I think I had spoken to...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Brian about the remediation that was needed to be done at that particular center.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I think it was mold remediation or asbestos remediation.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I forget exactly which one.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: But there was a concern about a possible closure because of the need to remediate.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So our priority is always...

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: to maintain center operations while we're doing repairs.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: And we work to make sure that can be done safely.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: If for some reason the work is extensive or if it has a life health safety component like asbestos or lead, then we may have to close down programming for the time of the repair and relocate programming somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: And we'll work with NYC Aging and our partners and the providers to make that happen.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: If it is a larger issue, like we had at, let's say, Latimer Gardens, where we're not able, it's not about a repair, it's about a major capital project, then we have to do a permanent shutdown.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how many times over the past year or five years an OAC was shuttered due to unsafe infrastructure. Trimble cites three examples: Glebe, Latimer, and Randall Avenue. She says Haber Center in Coney Island closed during Sandy and is still working on reopening, now needing a place of assembly permit.
chapters.title: Banks asks how many times OACs shuttered due to unsafe infrastructure

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Well, how many times over the past year or the past five years has the solution been to shutter OAC due to unsafe infrastructure concerns?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I have just those three examples, Glebe, Latimer, and Randall Avenue.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay, if an OAC is closed, how long on average does it take to reopen?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: It really depends, again, on the conditions.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Like Haber Center in Coney Island got closed down during Sandy, and we're still working on opening that.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We're on the last piece right now, which is the place of assembly permit.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So, you know, that one is obviously a very extreme example.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Glebe Avenue was closed down due to significant leak and mold conditions.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Luckily, that is going through the PAC program, and we'll receive comprehensive modernization, and we'll be able to reopen.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Just like we were able to reopen Edenwald after 25 years thanks to the POC program.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Congrats on that, yeah.

chapters.summary: Banks asks if a provider could make a repair proactively and seek reimbursement. McKenzie says it depends on the type of repair and additional funding sometimes allows NYC Aging to move forward. She says when sites shutter, NYC Aging ensures older adults have alternatives, including transportation to nearby sites.
chapters.title: Banks asks if providers can make repairs and seek reimbursement

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Could a provider make the repair or seek reimbursement if they needed to go ahead proactively and repair?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I would say it depends on the type of repair.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And as you know, as I just mentioned about the projects that we've completed, sometimes there is additional funding that comes in that allows us to be able to move forward with a repair.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And then, you know, we'll work together with NYCHA to be able to remove that from their listing.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: But I also want to just mention, when we do have to shutter one of the sites, we make sure immediately that our older adults do have alternatives.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: You know, they're not missing out on meals or programs that we will help them, even by providing transportation to nearby sites so that they do have programming that's available to them.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And my last question before I turn it back over to Chiz Wong.

chapters.summary: Banks asks if agencies are aware of OAC providers receiving fines or court summonses due to unresolved infrastructure issues at NYCHA properties. Trimble says they are aware of some violations tagged to OACs, some related to NYCHA repairs and some to provider responsibilities. She says NYCHA meets with providers to determine responsibility and cure violations.
chapters.title: Banks asks about fines and summonses against OAC providers

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Are the agencies aware of any OAC providers who received fines and old court summonses due to unresolved infrastructure issues?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: At the OAC facilities located on NYCHA properties.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We are aware of some violations that are tagged to the older adult centers.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Some of those violations are in relation to repairs that are NYCHA's response.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: or part of a capital program.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Some violations are assigned due to the provider's responsibility to make a repair or resolve a condition.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So again, it depends.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And how does the agencies assist the providers when this occurs?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We will meet with the provider and determine responsibility and how to cure the violation.

chapters.summary: Banks asks for a breakdown of violations. Trimble says there are currently 60 FDNY violations and two DOB violations at older adult centers. Banks asks how NYCHA is working to stop this from happening.
chapters.title: Banks asks for breakdown of FDNY and DOB violations

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Can you give us a breakdown?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I will find that information for you.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So right now we have 60 FDNY violations and two DOB violations at older adult centers.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how NYCHA will ensure this stops happening. Trimble says they cannot fully stop enforcement agency activities but will work with providers to cure violations once aware. Banks says faster response to complaints would help prevent providers from being dragged into court.
chapters.title: Banks presses on preventing violations and court appearances

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And how are you working to ensure that this stops happening?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I don't know if we can ever fully stop.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: These are important enforcement agency activities.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: But once we are aware of a violation, we will work with the provider to understand the conditions that have resulted and determine the best path forward to cure that violation.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I think this kind of goes back to the response and the time frame on when a complaint is put in and how quick you respond back to bringing some resolution to whatever the complaint may be.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I think that would be a much more appropriate response in making sure these types of things stop, where these providers have to be dragged into old court for this.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So hopefully you take that into consideration.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I'll turn it back over to the chair.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Zhuang thanks Banks and says she will give other council members a chance to ask questions. She calls on Council Member Elsie Encarnación. This is a procedural transition.
chapters.title: Zhuang transitions to other council members for questions

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And then we'll give chance to our other council members to ask questions.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: The first one we have council member.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And can I see you?

chapters.summary: Encarnación says she is new to older adult issues and asks basic questions about OAC contracts. She asks how funding is allocated for each center—by enrollment, square footage, or development population. McKenzie says it is all of the above and involves many metrics and parameters; NYC Aging can share the criteria.
chapters.title: Encarnación asks how OAC contract funding is allocated

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Hello.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So sorry.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I was not, I didn't know I was the first one.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So, you know, my predecessor, Deputy Speaker Ayala, she was the older adult whisperer.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So she had a lot more knowledge about older adults and what happens at the centers.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I don't have that much knowledge, so I just, excuse me for asking some basic baseline questions about the contracts.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: When it comes to the OAC contracts, can you explain how, like, funding is allocated for each center?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Is it based on enrollment like it is in school?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Is it based on square footage?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: How many people live in the development?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I just, to get an idea of how much.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I'd say all of the above.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: There's quite a few metrics and parameters that are included in the contract that would determine how much funding is allotted for each site.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We could share with you the criteria for that so that you have more information on it, but it's a lot more than just a couple of words.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Encarnación asks which services in the RFP are mandatory across programs. McKenzie says case management, food delivery, and activities/programs are mandatory, among others. She says NYC Aging will share the full list.
chapters.title: Encarnación asks which OAC services are mandatory in the RFP

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And then the services on the RFP, which ones are mandatory throughout each of the programs?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Are there any?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Yes, case management, obviously food delivery, activities and programs, several again.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So we'll share that with you as well.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Perfect.

chapters.summary: Encarnación notes the OAC RFP is coming soon and asks if there are info sessions that inform the RFP with older adults at the table. McKenzie says absolutely, there were several sessions and a concept paper. NYC Aging is still speaking with advocacy groups and elected officials about concerns.
chapters.title: Encarnación asks if RFP info sessions include older adults

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And then I noticed that you mentioned that the RFP for the OACs is coming up soon.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Are there info sessions that inform the RFP with older adults at the table?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: There were several sessions, and obviously there was also a concept paper.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: There was a lot of information and times for folks to collaborate along with older adults.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Even now, we're still speaking with some of our advocacy groups and some elected officials and so on on some of the concerns related to the upcoming OAC.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And so we are planning to have a meeting with them as well to further discuss some of their concerns.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Encarnación asks how long OAC contracts last and if they vary. McKenzie says they vary but are usually a year or two, later correcting that contracts are for three years with yearly extension options. She says there is oversight, audits, and periodic assessments by program officers.
chapters.title: Encarnación asks about RFP contract length and oversight

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And then, and how long is the RFP for that contract with the OACs?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Are they different?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
