utterances.text: Do they vary?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Yes, they do.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: But it's usually a year or two.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And through that year, there's, I don't know what you,

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I don't want to call them supervisions, but like...

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Yes, there's oversight throughout the period of the contract.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: There are also audits and obviously assessments by program officers on a periodic basis.

chapters.summary: Encarnación asks what top-line assessment points NYC Aging looks at after awarding an RFP. McKenzie says the assessment points are included in the contract and are not a surprise. She lists safety, volume of older adults served, and complaints or issues.
chapters.title: Encarnación asks what assessment points NYC Aging reviews

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Can you share some of the assessment points that you look at when...

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: You know, after awarding an RFP, what are some of the top line?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Things that you look at when you go in for those assessments?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Sure, and it's not a surprise thing.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: It's also included in the contract.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I thought you were going to share some top line right now.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Just like one or two things that you look at.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Safety, volume, how many older adults are actually being served, if there are complaints, issues.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I think my time is up, up.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: No.

chapters.summary: Encarnación says she is glad NYC Aging is looking at meatless options because seniors in her district do not go to centers on meatless day. She says the alternative options are terrible. McKenzie says older adults have been vocal and some travel to sites serving meat, so NYC Aging wants to meet their needs at preferred sites.
chapters.title: Encarnación raises concerns about meatless meal options

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And just I'm really glad to hear that you're looking at the meatless options.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: The seniors in my district cannot, they don't go to the senior centers when it's meatless day.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: And the options after that is terrible.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: So just.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I'm glad you're looking into that.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Well, thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: The older adults have, again, been very vocal about that, and they've also shared that they will find sites where meat is being served, and some of them may go there that day.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So we really want to be sure that we're meeting their needs at the sites they prefer.

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We have Council Member Abdul have questions.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I'm so sorry.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Before that, I just want to correct.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: The contracts are for three years, and they have an option to extend year by year.

chapters.summary: Council Member Amanda Farías asks about the JASA Throgs Neck Senior Center, which closed during COVID, reopened, then closed again due to mold and roof/HVAC damage. She says the center has been without a senior center for six years and asks when repairs and reopening can be expected. Trimble says the center is slated for PACT renovation, with project closing later 2027 and construction soon after.
chapters.title: Farías asks about JASA Throgs Neck Senior Center extended closure

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you for being here today.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: So I have a question about the Jasa Throgsnack Senior Center.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I always have a question about the Jasa Throgsnack Senior Center.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: It's faced an extended closure.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I mean, first they closed during COVID, and then they tried to reopen, closed again because they discovered mold.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Looks like the repairs started a year later, but they were stopped because there was additional, there was damage to the roof and additional structural damage and

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: needed roof repair and a replacement of the HVAC system from what I understand, just to start with.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And so they've been without a senior center for six years.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: That's a long time.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: If you know the Throgs Neck area, it's very, you know, kind of remote and far away, not easy to travel from.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And there was a temporary solution.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: They were using the Kiss Bay Boys and Girls Club, but then they were unable to use that.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Because of the kitchen situation and because the children, especially during the summer, they use the facility all day, every day for summer camp.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And have been trying to find a solution ever since nearby and have not found one.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Many of the seniors, I don't want to even say many, because many don't want to go all the way to Co-op City.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: To the senior center there.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: They don't like it.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: They don't like having to get on a bus or a shuttle to Co-op City so far away from their community.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And where the senior center is housed is in Randall,

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Balcom, where it's senior housing, but the entire Throgs Neck community really uses that senior center.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: So you have over 3,000 residents in Throgs Neck houses and Throgs Neck addition.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: And I'm using a low number here, but probably about a thousand seniors right now don't have access to a center.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: So I just want to know what is the, you know, because it's, you know, we were told it's now under packed.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: What's the situation there?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: When can we expect there to be repairs?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: When can we expect to have that senior center reopened again?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I'm familiar with the center and the decision to close it a few years back due to the significant conditions there.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: The center is slated to go through PACT and will receive full renovations as part of that.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: That project is anticipated to close later 2027, so it's still a little while away, and then construction would start soon after.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Um,

chapters.summary: Farías asks about DFTA's mental health initiative in over 80 OACs and wants the split among boroughs and how many are in the Bronx. McKenzie says she will get back on the Bronx split. She describes on-site services, a hub-and-spoke model, virtual services, and mobile options for sites without space.
chapters.title: Farías asks about mental health services split by borough

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: So through DIFTA's mental health initiative, we know that over 80 AOCs in New York City offer on-site and virtual mental health services.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Could you provide some information on where the split of those 80 OACs are amongst the five boroughs and how many are located in the Bronx?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I'll have to get back to you on the split of how many are located within the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: But I would say that, yes, it is another area that we're looking at to enhance geriatric mental health services.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Obviously, the sites that can have a center on site or provide those services on site are moving forward with that.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: But we do know that based on some of the requirements for this specific space, we will not be able to provide some of those services on site.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So where that's not possible, we do have a hub-and-spoke model where we make sure that folks that are located in areas that may not have an on-site center can access services through nearby

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: services at other sites, or they can receive those services virtually.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And we also provide supplemental service through Aging Connect at NYC Aging.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And one of the things that we're exploring is also looking at what we can do mobily, especially for those sites that will never be able to have an on-site

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: care program because of the constraints of space or privacy and so on.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So we are exploring that option as well because it might be something that I think could add to the services that are being provided to a...

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: allow an older adult to be able to access a service at that trusted space, but in a private space somewhere nearby.

chapters.summary: Farías says other senior centers are closer but not run by JASA, and asks if Throgs Neck seniors can go to Northeast Bronx Senior Center. McKenzie says any OAC participant can attend any of the 308 programs citywide. Farías notes JASA only transports to Co-op City, and McKenzie says NYC Aging will look into other transportation options.
chapters.title: Farías asks about transportation for Throgs Neck seniors to other centers

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Back to the senior center in Throgs Neck.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: There are other senior centers that are closer, but they're not run by JASA.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Is there any way?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: To allow for those seniors to go to like Northeast Bronx

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Senior Center, which is located right on Bruckner Boulevard, not far from, I mean it's far, but not as far as Co-op City, and it's a little easier to get to.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Any one of our OAC participants can attend any one of our programs, any one of the 308 throughout the city.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: They may opt to stay with JASA, but if they don't, they can go to any one of the centers and receive the same service.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Because JASA is only offering to transport them to Co-op City where their other site is, or I believe GLEEB.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Maybe JASA as well, but Co-op City is the one that they're transporting people to.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: It's something that we'll look into to see if there's some other services we can provide to ensure that older adults get to the centers they prefer.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I would like to follow.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: I'll go up with you on that.

chapters.summary: Farías cites DFTA's latest annual report showing 27 documented complaints about living conditions across 109 OACs in NYCHA-owned property. She asks what kinds of complaints were mainly received, how they were resolved, and how long resolution takes. McKenzie says average resolution is 12.8 days; Trimble says top complaints are paint, floors, walls, ceilings, and doors.
chapters.title: Farías asks about 27 documented complaints in annual report

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: According to DIFTA's latest annual report on older adult center metrics across 109 AOCs located in NYCHA-owned property, there were 27 documented complaints regarding living conditions.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Could you elaborate on the kind of complaints you were mainly receiving?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: How were they resolved, and how long do specific situations typically take to get resolved?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I'm sorry, are you saying these are living conditions?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Yes, OACs, locate, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: This was the conditions in the OACs, I apologize.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Okay, I think we've talked about the fact that it takes on average 12.8 days for any issue that's picked up at the sites.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I'm not sure if we're speaking outside of that framework that we've been talking about earlier, or is there something else?

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: No, just want to have a sense of what kind of complaints have you mainly been receiving and how long do those take typically?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So our typical complaints mirror some of the conditions in our residential buildings as well.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So we have paint issues, floors, walls, ceilings, and doors are the top five categories of complaints that we receive.

utterances.speaker: Amanda C. Farías
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And then next we have Council Member Hudson.

chapters.summary: Council Member Crystal Hudson recalls visiting William Hodson OAC at Butler Houses and seeing floorboards coming up, holes in ceilings, and lack of heat. She asks how NYC Aging determines a pipeline for OAC facilities needing capital improvements, whether some are prioritized, and how money moves. Trimble says NYCHA does not have a capital improvement pipeline for OACs; funding typically comes from elected officials for specific sites.
chapters.title: Hudson asks about capital improvement pipeline for OACs

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you so much, and good morning.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: When I chaired the Committee on Aging, I had the privilege of visiting many older adult centers across the city, as I know you have.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And one of those was the William Hudson OAC at Butler Houses up in Council Member Stevens'district in the Bronx.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: It also happens to be...

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: I suppose arguably the first senior center in the United States, and so certainly something to be proud about.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And so I'm wondering how you determine a pipeline for OAC facilities that are in need of capital improvements.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And my question really stems out of the conditions that I saw at the William Hodson OAC.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Everything from floorboards coming up, holes in the ceilings, lack of heat, I think, at times.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And so I'm just wondering what it takes for the pipeline to be created for or how you identify specific

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: sites to be on the pipeline, if there are some facilities that are given priority, how the money is moved, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We do not have a pipeline for capital improvements at older adult centers.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We are very grateful to the support we receive from the city council as well as other federal and state earmarks to support capital projects at our community centers.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So once funding is allocated, then we can implement the capital project, and the funding is typically identified for a specific site.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: It's not necessarily a pipeline that we choose.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So it comes from the elected official directly saying, I'd like to give money for this community center or this older adult center.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So that is right now the primary resource we have for doing comprehensive improvements outside of our pact conversions.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks if there are emergency funds for immediate needs. Trimble says emergency immediate repairs are different from comprehensive capital improvements. Life-health-safety repairs are responded to by NYCHA based on severity, but comprehensive improvements depend on allocated funding.
chapters.title: Hudson asks if there are emergency funds for immediate needs

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: And so no emergency funds for immediate needs?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So emergency immediate repairs would be different than a comprehensive capital improvement.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Just to be clear, if there's immediate repair needs that are life health safety, those are things that NYCHA does respond to based on the level of severity.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: But a comprehensive improvement in a capital project is based off of the allocation of funding.

chapters.summary: Hudson asks how much has been invested or set aside for William Hodson OAC. Trimble says she is not sure if she has that information for the specific center but can check and get back to her. Hudson asks her to follow up.
chapters.title: Hudson asks how much funding is earmarked for William Hodson OAC

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Do you know how much has been invested in?

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: set aside for earmarked for William Hudson OAC?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I have the information for that specific center, but we can check.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We can get back to you on any funding for that specific center.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Okay, that would be great.

utterances.speaker: Crystal Hudson
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Zhuang follows up asking whether leaks are emergency funding or regular capital. Trimble says it depends. Most leaks are repairs NYCHA will respond to, especially leaks from above in piping or roof. Leaks inside the center, like under a sink, are the provider's responsibility.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks if leaks are emergency or capital repairs

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I have a follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: For leaking, it's emergency funding or it's a regular capital?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: It depends.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So for the most part, a leak is a repair that we will respond to and make.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Again, especially if the leak is caused from a leak from above in our piping system, in our plumbing system, or a leak from our roof, that is something we will respond to and repair.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: If it's a leak that's within the center, like under the sink type leak, then the provider would get a plumber to fix that leak.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Next we have Council Member Brewer and followed by Council Member Rissler.

chapters.summary: Council Member Gale Brewer asks how RAD/PACT conversions impact repairs at OACs. Trimble says NYCHA works to include comprehensive modernization of centers in PACT financing, but it is not always possible. Section 8 rents cannot support community center renovation, so city subsidy is required.
chapters.title: Brewer asks how RAD/PACT conversions affect OAC repairs

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: A couple of things.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: One is with the rad pack because as you know on the Upper West Side I think we're pretty getting very rad packed.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So my question is if there's a center where there's a rad pack, how does that impact, if at all,

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: the issues at that center in terms of repairs?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So as part of our PAC program, we work hard to ensure that the centers also receive a comprehensive modernization, just like the apartments.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We will scope that out and do our best to include that in the financing.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Sometimes it's not always possible.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Sometimes we've had to take out the center.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: It really depends on the funding that's available for that project.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We cannot use Section 8 rents to support a community center renovation, so it would require city subsidy.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So as long as we have enough funding in the project, we will include the scope for the center to ensure that's part of the project as well.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We understand it's an important community resource.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We want to see it improved just alongside our apartments.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks how many conversions have included senior centers where NYCHA was able to do that. Trimble says she can confirm that number for her. Brewer moves to another question.
chapters.title: Brewer asks how many conversions included senior centers

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So do you have any sense of how many conversions have included senior centers where you have been able to do that?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I can confirm that number for you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Brewer notes it took five years to get the kitchen at Clinton at Harborview and asks how NYCHA handles proactive requests for new things. She asks how they plan for more seniors and needs like expansion or kitchens. McKenzie says NYC Aging has a running list of projects they are seeking funding for and will share it with the chair.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about proactive planning for new OAC needs like kitchens

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Number two, not under your leadership, but it took five years to get the kitchen at Clinton at Harborview.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So my question is, it's great to be, sounds like things are somewhat going well in terms of current requests, meaning the leak and so on.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But what about people and centers who want new things, proactive?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you have a list of those?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How does that get handled?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Kitchens would be one example of what I've always heard about.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In other words, how are we planning for the future?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: More seniors, obviously, and more needs.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I don't know if it's expansion, if it's a kitchen, if it's whatever.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How do we think about the future that way?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We have a running list of projects that we'd like to complete that we are actively seeking funding for.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I was able to mention earlier.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: that we have completed 56 projects and we're going to share a listing of those projects.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: In fact, I was able to speak with some of your colleagues in reference to, I think we should actually go and share with you some of the before and after of what's been accomplished by many of these

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: repairs and projects that include kitchens and bathrooms and things that seniors really appreciate.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So absolutely, there's a list of additional projects and areas we'd like to take a look at, including William Hudson, where I have visited.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And at William Hudson, they recently did have some upgrades to bathrooms and things like that.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Obviously, there's more work to be done.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: The work that can be done, we want to accomplish as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Can you get to the chair that list of what you'd like to accomplish?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We can share with you.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Brewer asks what metrics are used to assess the well-being of OAC infrastructure. McKenzie says DFTA uses an environmental checklist including leaks and plumbing, and program officers perform assessments. She says the information is included in the evaluation process and public portal. Trimble says NYCHA tracks open work orders and has a physical needs assessment estimating over $900 million in OAC capital needs.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about metrics for assessing OAC infrastructure well-being

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And the other question is, maybe you sort of discussed this, but so what are the metrics for assessing the well-being of this infrastructure?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Like how do you look at, you know, what you're doing and how do you measure that?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In terms of the centers?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Well, I'll say on the DFTA side, obviously we do have an environmental checklist that we use, things that we look at while we're there, which includes things like leaks and plumbing.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You're not there all the time.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I'm sorry?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You're not there all the time.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You're just one person.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Oh, no, this is included in the assessment also that the program officer is performing when they go out to the sites as well.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: You know, I'm a redundancy.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: You know, they're really the frontline staff that are carrying out the important critical work every day.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: and every week that they're out at the center.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So, yes, those are the things that we look at when we're there to ensure we have a safe, functional environment.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So where does that list go?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Is it like a list that goes on open data or is it kept internally?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: How do you address that list?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: It's included in the evaluation process for each of the sites, which is public.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: It's included in the portal and passport.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So we have that information.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And does DIFTA do the same in terms of metrics?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I mean, does NITRA do the same in terms of assessing metrics for the centers?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So we track our open work orders, and just like we do with our apartment repairs, we're tracking the work through that mechanism.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We also have our P&A, which estimates a need of just over $900 million for our older adult centers.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So, again, this is really a capital conversation more than a repair conversation.

chapters.summary: Brewer notes many centers have apartments above them and asks if individual apartment complaints are part of the discussion. McKenzie says DFTA only gets involved if it impacts the center, like a leak. She says caseworkers would escalate NYCHA-related issues for older adults through the biweekly meetings.
chapters.title: Brewer asks about individual apartments above OACs

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay, one other quick question.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Individual apartments.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I think a lot of your centers have apartments over them, not all, but many.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: And so I do.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: I have a lot of centers with apartments over them.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So my question is, as part of this discussion, are we also discussing the individual apartments?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: In other words, when people have complaints, and they do, they bring them to us, then what is that part of this overall metrics and how are we fixing them and that kind of thing?

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Do you look at that at the same time?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: From the DIFTA side, only if it impacts.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: our center.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So if it's something, a leak, then of course, right, then we would deal with NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: But if there's a noise complaint or something else that might impact services, obviously, yes, we would work along with NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: But if your caseworkers hear that Mrs.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Jones's mold is not being assessed and fixed, then I guess you would also hear about it.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: You bring it to NYCHA and we would go back and forth, then you call Gail.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: So I'm just saying, do you get some sense from your caseworkers that there is a responsiveness to the individuals living upstairs, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Absolutely there is.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And if they are not responsive, then that's where we fall into the framework that we discussed earlier, where we have those biweekly meetings with our liaison

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: and also with NITRA leadership and DIFTA leadership so that we can address something that may be outside of our purview, obviously, if an

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: older adult in one of our centers is having a problem that's a NITRA-related issue, but we would certainly escalate it to NITRA's attention that this older adult needs help and these are the issues that are concerning them.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Gale A. Brewer
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We have Council Member Ressler and followed by Council Member Osei.

chapters.summary: Council Member Lincoln Restler asks about the status of a pause on council allocations for NYCHA capital projects a few years ago. Eva Trimble calls up Deputy Chief Asset and Capital Management Officer Abigail Fradkin. Fradkin says NYCHA is accepting all council capital funding now; a temporary pause due to staffing shortage has been resolved.
chapters.title: Restler asks about pause on council allocations for NYCHA capital projects

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chair Zhuang and Chair Banks, for this important hearing.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Good to see you, Chief Operating Officer and Commissioner.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Appreciate you guys being here today and for your hard work.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Could I just get clarification?

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: There was a pause place.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: on council allocations for NYCHA capital projects a few years ago.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: What's the status of that?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I'm going to call up our Deputy Chief Asset and Capital Management Officer, Abigail Fragkin, to talk about that.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: We are currently accepting all funding that the City Council is able to provide for capital work at NITRA, including older adult centers.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: There was a temporary pause on projects that had previously been funded due to a staffing shortage, and we've been able to restart all of those projects and are currently accepting any funding that is available to us.

chapters.summary: Restler says Brooklyn Borough President allocated $6 million in FY24 for upgrades to older adult centers, primarily on NYCHA campuses, but has received no updates. He asks if it is standard to have no updates two years later. Fradkin says that is not standard and asks for the specific list to look into it. Restler says he will provide it and expects updates this week.
chapters.title: Restler asks about Brooklyn BP $6M allocations and lack of updates

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Great.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So I'm fortunate to have a great borough president in Brooklyn, the best borough president in the best borough.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Sorry, Gail.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And he allocated $6 million in FY24 for upgrades to older adult centers, primarily on NYCHA campuses.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But he's got no information, no updates on the timeline for those projects.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Is that standard practice two years later to not have updates on capital allocations that are made to NYCHA older adult centers?

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: That is not standard practice.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: If you could share the specific list of allocations, we can definitely look at that.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: Sometimes there is insufficient funding that has been allocated to address the needs at a center.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: And so in that case, we might be working with the borough president.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: or city council member to ensure that there is the full amount of funding available before we actually accept the funding and move forward with initiating a project.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I mean, I'll just be clear in going back and forth with him, his budget director, his senior staff.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: They've had no communication or updates from NYCHA on this.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So if there's a funding gap, it'd be news to them.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: But we're happy to hear that you will be moving forward on them and that you'll be providing updates to the Borough President's Office this week on those projects.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So thank you very much for your willingness to work with us on the follow-ups.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Those cover my questions for today.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I want to thank everybody.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: Thank both agencies for their hard work here.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: I know that this is not an easy topic.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And I want to congratulate the rat, Zarina, for landing on her feet.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: And it's always good to see Brian Honan.

utterances.speaker: Lincoln Restler
utterances.text: So thank you all.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Please send the list to us also.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And also, we have Council Member Chioze.

chapters.summary: Council Member Chi Ossé asks how the lack of federal investment in public housing tangibly impacts older adult centers on NYCHA campuses. Trimble says HUD appropriations were cut by 14% last year, making it harder for NYCHA to maintain operations. Repair needs at OACs compete with the same plasterers and plumbers needed for resident apartments, so response times may lengthen.
chapters.title: Ossé asks how federal funding cuts impact NYCHA OACs

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Chairs.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Nice to see you all this morning.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: I wanted to first start by obviously addressing how this federal government is not investing in public housing, and obviously that's impacting NYCHA across the board.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: And I was just interested in the lack of funds that we are seeing from the federal government.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: How is that?

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Tangibly impacting our older adult centers on our NITRA campuses.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Obviously, we are always advocating in D.C.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: For additional funding.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: The HUD appropriations, and Brian can correct me if I'm wrong, were cut by 14% last year.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: And so it is a struggle for NYCHA to continue the same level of operating with decreasing federal funding.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: And that filters down to everything we do.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So if we have needs for plastering or plumbing at an older adult center, that is competing with the same plasterer and plumber that needs to respond to a resident in their apartment.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So it will mean that the time to respond will continue to get longer.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: And I appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: And, you know, obviously I hope things change within that regard because we know that that nature does need that support from from the feds.

chapters.summary: Ossé asks how many HVAC inspections NYCHA conducts at older adult centers, especially in his district, and how often. Trimble says NYCHA does not conduct HVAC inspections; HVAC is mostly the provider's responsibility. McKenzie adds that NYC Aging performs pre-tests before cooling and heating seasons and has not identified issues preventing heat this winter.
chapters.title: Ossé asks about HVAC inspections at OACs

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: But I did want to ask, because we are going into a cold winter, maybe hopefully not as cold as as last year.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: I wanted to ask how many.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: of HVAC inspections NYCHA is doing across the board, but mostly within our older adult centers on the grounds of my district.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: How often are those inspections taking place?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We do not conduct HVAC inspections.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: The HVAC is the responsibility of the provider for the most part.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: There are some instances where NYCHA would be involved, but for the most part, the HVAC system is the responsibility of the provider.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: And does NYCHA provide any oversight over the providers?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: No, the providers are contracted by New York City.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: But at New York City Aging, we do perform pre-tests before cooling season and before heating season to assess if there are any issues that would prevent us from providing heat for the winter.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We're in that process right now, and we have not been made aware of any projects or needs that would keep us from providing heat at our sites.

chapters.summary: Ossé asks how often mold inspections occur at older adult centers. Trimble says NYCHA inspects based on a mold request work ticket and will provide the response timeframe. McKenzie says DFTA does surface inspections during environmental checklists but asks NYCHA to confirm mold.
chapters.title: Ossé asks about mold inspections at OACs

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: And furthermore, how many rounds of mold inspection take place, or how often does the mold inspection at our older adult centers?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We will inspect based on a mold request work ticket.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So if the center submits a work ticket to NYCHA for mold, we will come and we will do that inspection.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I don't have the time frame to respond, but I will get that for you.

utterances.speaker: Chi A. Ossé
utterances.text: Does the Department of Aging do that as well for OAC?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: It would be a surface inspection during our environmental checklist if there were mold or any material that we find that needs to be investigated.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We wouldn't determine that it's mold.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: That's something that we would ask NYCHA to do.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Thank you, chairs.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks how power outages at OACs are handled. Trimble says NYCHA emergency services works with providers, sends robocalls, and coordinates with NYC Aging to make accommodations. During this summer's outages, they sometimes referred people to nearby centers. Zhuang asks if NYCHA or DFTA handles it; Trimble says it is a partnership.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about power outages at OACs

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And the follow-up question.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So we test the heat and the cooling system.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: If there's any emergency,

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Outage, power outage, do we have any way to deal with that in the OACs?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: When we experience a power outage, NYCHA's emergency services works with the provider to provide information.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We send out robocalls just as we do with our residents.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: And, you know, depending on the length of outage, we will work with NYC Aging and the provider to make accommodations as needed.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: This summer we had quite a few instances of power outages, and so we'll sometimes refer to nearby centers as needed.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: And it really depends on the length and the condition of the outage.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So is this always a different handle this issue or it's a NITRA handle this issue?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: It's in partnership.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So if it's an outage that's impacting our buildings, we will coordinate with the provider and with NYC Aging to ensure that programs can continue somewhere.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: And then we'll make sure that we're giving them information as to the length of the outage, the cause, and any restoration times.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks if all OACs on NYCHA campuses are ADA compliant. Trimble says no, they are not all ADA compliant. Zhuang asks if there is a plan to bring facilities up to standard. McKenzie says as many as possible, but it requires capital investment; interim measures are used where needed.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks if all NYCHA OACs are ADA compliant

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Are all OACs on NITRA campus ADA compliant?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: No, they are not all ADA compliant.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Is there a plan in place to bring those facilities up to standard?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I'd say as many as possible.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Again, it would be a capital investment for some of the sites to be able to bring them up to ADA compliancy.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So for the sites that are not ADA compliant, we do work along with the older adults there to see if there are any interim measures that we need to put in place.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: But the plan would be to make that investment, obviously, when funding is allotted and to continue with the projects.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks if ADA compliance can be put in next year's budget. McKenzie says if the council is willing, absolutely. Zhuang asks how many of the 105 NYCHA OACs are not ADA compliant. Trimble says they do not have that number but can see if they have the information.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks to put ADA compliance in next year's budget

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Can we put that to next year's budget?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: If you're willing, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We're going to ask the mayor, right?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: They're also from 105 OAC facility located in Niche.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: How many are not ADA compliant?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We don't have that number, but I can see if we have that information.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks how DFTA coordinates with NYCHA to ensure ADA compliance and make necessary changes. McKenzie says through capital enhancements and available funding. Zhuang asks for details on funding needed, how many centers are compliant, and costs. McKenzie says not at the moment; they would need to assess each site with NYCHA.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks how DFTA coordinates with NYCHA on ADA compliance

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: How is DFTA coordinated with NITRA Insure ADA compliant?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And make the necessary change.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Through the capital enhancements.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And again, if we're able to effect any projects that would allow us to be able to

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: to resolve the issue of ADA compliancy, we're willing to do that with the available funding.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And also, do you able to provide us all the detail, how much funding we need, how many center already ADM compliant, how many not, how much the cost?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Not at the moment.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Obviously, along with NYCHA, we'd have to look at the number of sites and what are the circumstances at each one of those sites to determine how much each project would cost, and then you would get an overall cost from that.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: And we can also discuss with the council what that means.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: There's different levels of compliance with ADA requirements, whether it's wheelchair accessibility or bathroom accessibility.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: There's different components, and that would require different levels of scope.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So we'd have to do a pretty significant assessment of all the centers to determine the full need.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks what security protocols protect older adults at OACs on NYCHA property. Trimble says NYCHA does not provide security at OACs. McKenzie says most sites collaborate with NYPD for patrols and use door locking mechanisms, intercoms, or swipe systems. Staff receive training and communicate with NYPD about neighborhood issues.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about security protocols at NYCHA OACs

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And I give recent concerns about safety at some nature property.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: What security protocol are in place to protect other adults at?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: Those OACs.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: NITRA does not provide security at the OACs.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So for our sites, most of them we are in collaboration with NYPD for patrols of those areas.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: In addition to most of our centers are secured by some type of door locking mechanism, whether it's intercom system or it's door swipes, to ensure that we're just not allowing everyone in without someone

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: being aware of who's coming into the center.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So we look at different security precautions.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We do have training for our staff.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We also speak to them about some of the issues in the neighborhood.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Obviously, our older adults will let us know if there are issues in the neighborhood, and we would collaborate with NYPD.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Yes, NYPD has, each person has a person signed for senior issues?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: No, but they have a community affairs division that would allow us to have patrols of those particular sites that might have some issues.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks for an outline of the current state of facilities housing OACs and measures taken to address infrastructure concerns. She asks how many are in good condition versus not. McKenzie says they can share that information but do not have it on hand today.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks for outline of current facility conditions and infrastructure measures

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, can you provide outline of risk?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Of current state of facilities housing OACs and what measures are being taken to address infrastructure concerns?

utterances.speaker: Elsie Encarnación
utterances.text: I'm sorry, could you repeat that?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Can you provide an outline of current state of facility housing OACs and what measures are taken to address infrastructure?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: concerns.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So the entire, the overview of the environmental assessment of all sites?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: How many are, you think it's in good condition?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: How many you think it's not in good condition?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Do you have any information about those?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We could share that with you.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I don't have it on hand today.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Zhuang cites reports that Latimer Gardens OAC, serving around 700 seniors, was closed due to persistent roof leaks. She asks how NYCHA and DFTA responded. Trimble says the facility was closed and programming relocated. Fradkin says the roof project is not currently funded; if funded, it would take about four years.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about Latimer Gardens OAC closure due to roof leaks

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Recent reports highlight that the issues in one of the OAC centers in NITCHER campus,

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: like a Vladimir Garden OAC, which served around 700 seniors, the inflation was closed due to persistent roof leaks.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: How did the NITCHER and the DFTA respond?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Yes, we were, it was unfortunate that we had to close that facility.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We had been working to make repairs for a while, but the repairs were significant and it was determined by aging and the provider that it was the best resource right now was to relocate the site and the programming.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: When did you guys start notice that the leaking issue in that center?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I don't know when.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: It's an issue with the roof.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: It would require a full roof replacement.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So it has been ongoing for a while.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: How long did it take to do the repair?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: The roof project is not currently funded.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So you're not doing anything in that project.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: People just have to move to other centers.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: The center is closed.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: We're currently in discussions with a funder to identify funding for the full roof replacement, but that has not yet been confirmed.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: If the funding for the full roof replacement were to be confirmed, it would be a project that would take about four years.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Four years?

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: If they have funding, take four years.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So that's going to run the same problem as a senior center in Council Member Audubon's district.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: Capital work is typically extensive.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: Spanning from the planning and design phase to the procurement phase to the actual construction work.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, what's the response of DFTA if this is a situation like this?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Well, it's unfortunate that this situation occurred, but obviously recognizing that leaving the older adults at that site would be a severe health and safety concern.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We did act to relocate those older adults to a center that was safer for them.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: They're receiving the same programs and services at the relocation site as they would at the closed site.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So 700 seniors get to the same service?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: They may not be at the same relocation site.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Obviously, there may be more than one that they are availing themselves of the services, but they are availing themselves of the services at another site.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: For me, the DIFTA response is primarily to keep our older adults safe, and that's what we did.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks if there is a plan to inspect every OAC on NYCHA campuses to prevent similar situations. Trimble says there is no plan to inspect each site, but NYCHA's physical needs assessment estimates OAC capital improvement costs at approximately $900 million. Zhuang then asks for borough breakdown of the 105 OACs.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks if NYCHA will inspect every OAC to prevent closures

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Is there any plan to inspect every single OACs located in NITRA campus to prevent this type of situation happening?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We don't have a plan to do an inspection of each of our sites, but as I mentioned before, right now as part of our physical needs assessment, which is our overall capital assessment for all of NYCHA,

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: we estimate the capital improvement costs for our older adult centers to be approximately $900 million.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks how many OACs are in each borough. Trimble says the 105 breaks down as Bronx 26, Manhattan 30, Brooklyn 35, and Queens/Staten Island 14. Zhuang confirms Brooklyn has 35. She then asks how many are at PACT sites versus Section 9.
chapters.title: Trimble provides borough breakdown of 105 NYCHA OACs

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We know there's 105 property OACs located in NITRA property.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Do you have how many each borough?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Yes, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: The 105 breaks out as Bronx 26, Manhattan 30, Brooklyn 35, and Queens Staten Island 14.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: How many in Brooklyn?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks how many OACs are at PACT sites and how many remain in Section 9. Trimble says 77 centers are in NYCHA's Section 9 portfolio and 28 are in the PACT portfolio. As PACT conversions continue, the number in Section 9 will decrease and PACT will increase.
chapters.title: Trimble says 77 OACs in Section 9 and 28 in PACT portfolio

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: How many are at PAC sites and how many remain in Section 9?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We have 77 centers in NYCHA's Section 9 portfolio and 28 in our PAC portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Has the number of OAC at PAC site increased or decreased over the past five years?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Yes, as we continue to convert sites through PAC, the number of centers will decrease in the NYCHA Section 9 portfolio and increase in the NYCHA PAC portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: What counts for any change?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: The PAC conversions.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Only because conversion, we have to change the senior center?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We don't change the senior center.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: It's just part of the PAC program versus part of NYCHA's Section 9 program.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Got it.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks how many older adults are served by OACs on NYCHA property. McKenzie provides citywide breakdown: Bronx 8,212 (35.5%), Brooklyn 8,314 (22.3%), Manhattan 14,540 (41.7%), Queens 6,490 (14.1%), and Staten Island 2,095 (32.8%). Zhuang then asks for meal and mental health service breakdowns.
chapters.title: McKenzie provides borough breakdown of older adults served by NYCHA OACs

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: How many other adults are served by OAC located in NYCHA property?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We have the citywide breakdown.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: By Boremi.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: In Bronx, it's 35.5% or 8,212.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: In Brooklyn, 8,314, 22.3%.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Queens, 6,490 or 14.1%.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And in Staten Island, 2,095 or 32.8%.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks how many meal services, mental counseling, and other related services are provided in each center or borough. McKenzie says NYC Aging will provide a breakdown. She notes they provide 6.3 million meals overall and will break out mental health services.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks for meal and mental health service breakdowns by borough

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: How many meal services and mental counseling and other related services in each center or each borough?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Was that meal service and services?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We'll give you more, a breakdown of them.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Obviously, we know we're providing 6.3 million meals overall, so we have to give you the breakdown.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And also mental health counseling.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And mental health services.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Does this, so you're going to send us the data, right?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Yes, we will.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Definitely.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks whether older adults typically live in the NYCHA facility where the OAC is located or travel from elsewhere. McKenzie says NYC Aging wishes more participants were residents of the NYCHA facilities, but there has been a dip in participation from people living in the building. Centers are serving more of the surrounding community, and NYC Aging convened tenant association meetings to address barriers.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks whether OAC participants live in the NYCHA facility or travel

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Do these older adults typically live in NITRA facility, which the OAC is located, or do some travel from other locations such as NITRA facility or private housing?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We wish there were more participants that are residents in the NITRA facilities, but we have noticed that there's a dip in the participation from persons that are living right in the building.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And these centers are servicing more of the surrounding community, which is one of the reasons why we convened the first ever meeting along with the Tenant Association, so that we could work together to boost those numbers and find out what are the barriers to

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: people that are right in the same building coming down to our centers.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks the current ratio of staff to OAC members at NYCHA campuses. McKenzie says she does not have the ratio and will get it. Zhuang asks how the city ensures staff meet older adults' needs and what role DFTA plays in staffing.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about staff-to-member ratio at NYCHA OACs

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: What are current ratio of staff to OAC members to OAC located in NITRA campus?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I don't have the ratio of staff.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I'll get that for you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks how the city ensures staff meet older adults' needs and DFTA's role in staffing. McKenzie says DFTA has staff on site daily, weekly supervisory staff, and the commissioner visits centers. She recently onboarded DFTA's first chief quality officer to analyze data and focus on outcomes.
chapters.title: McKenzie describes DFTA staffing oversight and new chief quality officer

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: How can city ensure the staff meet the needs of these older adults?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: What role does DIFTA play in staffing?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And again, it goes back to the monitoring, as I've mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We have staff on site daily.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We have weekly supervisory staff that are out at the centers.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Obviously, I'm visiting the centers as well.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And we're closely monitoring the metrics.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: One additional provision that we provided very recently, I've onboarded the very first chief quality officer for DFTA so that we could take a deeper dive into the data that's available.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Obviously, we have an extensive amount of data, but we want to be sure that we're focusing on the outcomes and how we're really affecting the lives of older adults.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So you guys already doing...

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Like feedback from NITRA and also OACs.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Absolutely.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks if feedback from NYCHA and OACs is shared with NYCHA. McKenzie says yes, at senior leadership meetings they discuss issues impacting OACs and ways to improve. She gives examples: 88% of escalated issues resolved, some faster than 12.8 days, and collaboration on capital projects.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks if OAC feedback is shared with NYCHA and examples of improvement

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Is the feedback shared with NITRA?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: At our meeting where we meet with the senior leaders, we speak about issues that impact the OACs and also ways that we can improve and enhance our services together.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Is there any issue or example you can give to us after you get the feedback from the OACs and communicate with NITRA and any improvement?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: I can give you two.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: One is where I mentioned that we've resolved 88% of the issues that we've escalated to NITRA and that those issues have been resolved, some of them even earlier than the 12.8 days that it typically takes to improve something.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And then also...

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And the fact that we've been able to look at issues together, we have been able to look at capital projects where perhaps there's a portion of the project that we might be able to affect the repair.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So we feel in this collaboration, in this enhanced relationship that we have, it not only presents opportunities, but it's also helping us to provide better services.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks how often NYC Aging does outreach to engage older adults in NYCHA residents at OACs. McKenzie says on the DFTA side it is continuous. She mentions the first-ever meeting with the tenant association and residents to better understand needs.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about outreach to older adults in NYCHA OACs

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: How often are you guys doing outreach effort to engage with older adults in NITRA residents at OACs?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: On the DIFTA side, it's continuous.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And as I mentioned, we had that first ever meeting with the tenant association and several of the residents of the building also attended to help us to better understand what we could do to meet their needs in an enhanced way.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Let me turn to the floor to Council Chair Banks.

chapters.summary: Banks returns to fines and asks if an OAC provider pays a fine, are they reimbursed. Trimble says it depends on the specific incident and whether the violation is the provider's responsibility. Banks asks about NYCHA-caused violations; Trimble says she is not familiar with reimbursement and NYCHA would work to correct it.
chapters.title: Banks asks if OAC providers are reimbursed for fines

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I guess I want to dive right into Rad Pack, particularly with the conversions that continue to take place, and I guess more obviously down the line.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: For developments undergoing PAC conversion, well, let me back up because I needed to get this on the record as well.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Going back to the OACs that have received fines or been going into oath, when a fine is issued to an OAC provider and it's paid by the provider,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: are they reimbursed?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: It depends.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I'd have to understand the specific incident, but again, there are certain violations that are the provider's responsibility, and so if they do not correct it, is there fine to pay?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay, so it's case by case based on what I'm...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And for nitrous ones?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I'm not familiar with reimbursement.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: They probably wouldn't pay.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We'd work to correct it.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Banks asks if NYCHA coordinates with the new private management company to ensure OAC services are maintained post-rehabilitation. Trimble says yes, NYCHA conducts extensive outreach before conversion and connects community facilities with the incoming development team. Centers do not experience a gap in operations because they are funded by NYC Aging.
chapters.title: Banks asks if NYCHA coordinates with new PAC management on OAC services

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: For developments undergoing PAC conversions, does NYCHA coordinate with the new private

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: management company to ensure that the OAC services are maintained post-rehabilitation?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So as we do with our residents, we conduct extensive outreach and engagement prior to a conversion, and that includes making sure our partners in the development are also connected.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So if there's an OAC or a community center or any other type of community facility, we work to make sure they are connected with the incoming development team, which would be their new landlord, to make sure they understand how to escalate, how to work together, and make those connections.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: The centers do not experience any gap in...

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: In operations as part of the PAC conversion.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Everything continues because they are funded by NYC Aging to continue to operate their services regardless of the conversion.

chapters.summary: Banks says Boulevard Houses had a gap of about a year and a half outside its center, with services moved to an apartment. He asks what NYCHA is doing to assist community entities in getting services back and what conversations are happening with the RAD/PACT partner. Trimble says they are not forgotten and work to ensure continuity, but relocations may be needed during modernization.
chapters.title: Banks raises Boulevard Houses gap in services after RAD/PACT

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Boulevard Houses went through a long gap, I think close to two years of being, about a year and a half probably, of being outside their center.
