utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: There was a gap in services there because the location where, and this is not a DIFTA funded program, but nevertheless it's under RADPAC.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: The services where they were moved to, or the building that they were moved to, obviously it was an apartment.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: In a situation like that, what is NITRA doing to assist those particular entities that's in the community?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: community center to get the services back?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What's the conversation with the Rad Pack partner?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What's going on?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Because sometimes it feels as though they're just forgotten about.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: No, they're definitely not forgotten about.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Our intent is always to ensure continuity of services and programs, whether it's a senior center or another community facility.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: There are situations where we have to have a relocation or a break-in service in order to do the important modernization work that the buildings are undergoing.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So if we're replacing full plumbing, electricity, things like that, we may have to shut down services to a building, and that would involve relocating a program during that construction period.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: When we are relocating a program, we are working closely with the city agency, whether it's NYC Aging or DIFTA,

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: and the providers to identify alternative locations for that program to make sure that the residents are still able to benefit from it during the construction period.

chapters.summary: Banks asks if the deals or agreements for community centers in each RAD/PACT program are shaped the same. Trimble says no, they are very deal-specific. Banks then asks how many of the 28 PACT developments have been rehabbed.
chapters.title: Banks asks if RAD/PACT deals for community centers are standardized

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And each deal, I mean, are they modeled after the same between the community center from each RADPAC program?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Are the deals normally shaped the same or the agreements?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: No, they are very deal specific.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay, do I?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how many of the 28 PACT developments have gone through renovation. Trimble says she will have to get that number. Banks asks if rehab of community centers is part of the agreement or a requirement. Trimble says it is not required, but it is always NYCHA's intent to improve community spaces alongside apartments.
chapters.title: Banks asks how many PACT developments have been rehabbed

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How many NITRA developments have been rehabbed?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Well, sorry, how many PAC developments that have been rehabbed?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Out of the 28, how many have been to rehab, have gone through a renovation?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I will have to get you that number.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I don't have that available today.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Is that part of the agreement?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Or is that one of the requirements?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: It's not required, but it's always our intent to improve the community spaces alongside our residential apartments.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We understand the importance of that.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So we work to include the scope of work for those centers as part of the overall comprehensive modernization of the site.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: However, it really is deal specific as to what the deal can cover and the cost of those renovations.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So, for example, the Section 8 funding cannot be used to cover the cost of a community center, so we have to rely on city subsidy to cover the cost of community spaces.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So it really depends on how much funding the project can support in order to see how much work we can do in the centers.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So there are centers or community centers that have OACs in them that have not been rehabbed.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Or have not received full rehab.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I have not received rehab.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: It's possible, but I'll get you those numbers.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how the RAD/PACT partner deals with needed investments in centers that have not been rehabbed. Trimble says the new landlord would be responsible for making repairs to ensure continuity of services. Banks says it is interesting that rehabbing centers is not a requirement.
chapters.title: Banks asks how RAD/PACT partners handle needed investments in centers

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So how was the RADPAC partner then dealing with the needed investments that's needed in those particular centers?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Were they just allowed to just exist?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: They would continue to make their repairs in order to ensure continuity of services.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So the Rad Pack partner would be responsible for making those repairs?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Yes, as the new landlord, they would be responsible for making the repairs in the centers.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: That's really interesting that that's not a requirement to rehab these centers.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Because obviously if you're rehabbing an apartment, it would make sense that you would rehab the centers or just like any other commercial spaces that may be a part of the night to develop.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: It's always included in our scope at the start.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: However, again, the...

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: The resources that are required to do these projects may mean that we don't have enough funding to do a full scope for the centers.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Our priority is the apartments.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Banks asks what happens to capital funds allocated by the council for an OAC site if the development later transitions to RAD/PACT. Trimble says it is case-by-case and eligibility varies. Fradkin says if work has begun, it continues; if not begun, NYCHA works with the funder to determine whether funding continues or is repurposed.
chapters.title: Banks asks what happens to council capital funds if a development converts to RAD/PACT

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And then what about when it comes to when a conversion is done,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: what happens to capital funds allocated to the NITRA development that were approved by the council for an OAC site if that development then later transitions to RADPAC?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: What happens to those funds?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So similar to what we said before on a case-by-case basis, each PAC site is different, and eligibility for capital improvements varies.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: between the sites.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So it needs to be determined on a case-by-case basis.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We will take a look at what was allocated, what the need is, and we will work together to try to ensure that those funds can go to the site, but we can't guarantee it.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: But is there, I mean, obviously there's been converting developments.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: There should be a track record or at least something that exists already.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: To show how you've dealt with those situations where there has been monies allocated.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I just want to make sure that these centers are not losing funding when a conversion does take place.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: Yeah, I mean, it does depend on, it is done on a case-by-case basis.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: So if there is already a renovation that is where funding has been allocated and the work has begun at the older adult center, then that work would continue and would be coordinated with the renovation work happening as part of the PAC conversion.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: If the funding was allocated but the project has not yet begun, then on a case-by-case basis, we'd work with

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: the city council member or whoever the funder was for that work to determine whether that funding should continue to be allocated for

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: that center as part of the conversion or whether it should be repurposed for another project in our Section 9 portfolio.

chapters.summary: Banks asks if there is a possibility the center could lose funding during a conversion that is supposed to help the development. He notes there may not be enough funding for center rehabs. Trimble says anything is possible, but NYCHA's intent is to leverage all resources for community and residential properties. She cannot guarantee no site has ever lost money.
chapters.title: Banks asks if centers can lose funding during conversion

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So there's a possibility that the center could actually lose funding, do a conversion that's supposed to help the development.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And then keep in mind, too, that you're

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: You said that it's a possibility that there may not be enough funding to do the rehabs in the center.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So is that taken into consideration too?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Everything, all of the above.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Anything is possible, but our intent is to always work to leverage all of the resources we have for the benefit of our properties, both community and residential.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I can't guarantee that no site has ever lost money, but that's definitely not something we would ever like to see happen.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So we work with the city council.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We work with OMB.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We try to make these deals work as best as we can.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: But again, it depends on the scope and the timing of the funding in comparison to when the project is going through construction.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Has there been any situations where...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Funding has been taken away or lost.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I'd have to get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I'm not as familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Can you give me...

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We will get back to you.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Um,

chapters.summary: Banks notes NYCHA has said PAC partners and OAC providers sign lease agreements assigning repair responsibilities. He asks how many are in effect. Trimble says only a handful are in place; it is not required but encouraged. NYCHA shared a template with NYC Aging.
chapters.title: Banks asks how many PAC lease agreements are in effect

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: In the past, NITRA has stated that PAC partners and OAC providers sign lease agreements that assign repair responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How many of these lease agreements are in effect?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So we do encourage the providers and the PAC partners to work together to finalize a lease agreement.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: There's only a handful in place right now.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: It's not a requirement that the provider sign the agreement, but we think it's good business practice and we encourage it.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We've shared a template that we've worked on with NYC Aging as well.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So there's a template, okay.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So that we think it's an important tool, but it's not required, but we do have a handful already.

chapters.summary: Banks asks if NYCHA monitors compliance with these agreements. Trimble says NYCHA is not a party to those agreements. NYCHA provides oversight of the PACT program and escalates issues about OACs if they arise. Banks asks how many disputes have been reported.
chapters.title: Banks asks if NYCHA monitors compliance with PAC lease agreements

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Does NITRA monitor compliance with these agreements?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Or whatever agreement that they come to, does NITRA monitor those agreements?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We're not a party to those agreements.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So, you know, in our general monitoring of our...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: When do you provide oversight?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We provide oversight of the PACT program.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: And so if there are issues that are escalated about a...

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Older adult center, then, you know, we would, those issues would get escalated.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We'd take a look at them and we'd work together with the provider, NYC Aging, to resolve them.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So the components of the agreement is not monitored, you know, by an

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: There's no oversight over the different components.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We're not a party to that agreement.

chapters.summary: Banks asks how many disputes have been reported. Trimble says she does not have information on any disputes and will see if NYCHA has that information. Banks then asks if there are surveys of centers converted to RAD/PACT.
chapters.title: Banks asks about disputes under PAC lease agreements

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: How many disputes have been reported?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I don't have information on any disputes.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Can you get us those numbers on the disputes?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I will see if we have that information.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And I'm going to turn this over back to my chair.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I think I had one more question.

chapters.summary: Banks asks if surveys have been taken at centers converted to RAD/PACT to assess whether the experience has been good or bad. McKenzie says NYC Aging has not surveyed yet, but she has visited some converted centers and older adults were thrilled. She says the environment is greatly enhanced by RAD/PACT.
chapters.title: Banks asks if surveys assess RAD/PACT converted centers

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Oh, are there any surveys taken from these particular centers that have been converted over to Rad Pack?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Just to get a sense of if the experience has been good, bad.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We haven't taken a survey of it yet on the New York City aging side, but I can tell you, having visited some of the recently converted, the older adults were thrilled.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: It is a much enhanced environment.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Early on, you mentioned some of the complaints and, you know,

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Councilmember Hudson mentioned having floorboards coming up and holes in the ceilings and those types of things at some of the sites that she's visited.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: The environment is greatly, greatly enhanced by the Rad Pack program.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: And I'll say, as we're on our tour, the Rad Pack manager, whoever it is for that particular site, has also joined us on the tour.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: They seem very invested in making sure that they're protecting the program.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: property and also providing a great environment for the older adults.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So thus far, we're very pleased with what we see, but we'll continue to monitor.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Yeah, it would be nice if you can survey them.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I would love to hear what they have to say.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Thank you, Chair.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks about large city capital funding for NYCHA, such as $221.9 million for lead abatement in FY27, and whether any is used for OAC repairs. Trimble says those line items are mostly for apartments, not community centers. Community centers primarily benefit from direct allocations from elected officials, not NYCHA's capital plan.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks how much city capital funding goes to OAC repairs

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I have some questions about the budget.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: A large amount of city capital funding at NYCHA received goes towards lump sum projects such as lead abatement, which funded at $221.9 million in fiscal 2027

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: adopted budget.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Other examples of these are asbestos abatement.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Comprehensive approach to mold, general construction, and the building improvement.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We want to know which and if there's a large part for capital funding are being used for facilitate repairs in older adult centers.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Thank you, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: For the most part, those line items you're referencing are for our apartments and not for our community centers.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: As I mentioned earlier, the community centers primarily benefit from direct allocations from elected officials in the council or state or federal partners.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: They are not part of our capital plan.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So even you get the money, you guys are not going to improve any senior center.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Even in the same building, you are doing second floor, you will not do first floor.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: The centers obviously benefit from work we're doing on our buildings.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: If we're repairing our roofs, if we're repairing our heating systems, if we're doing building line initiatives for replacement of plumbing stacks, centers in those buildings would benefit from it.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: But the...

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Those funding lines that you mentioned are primarily for the benefit of our apartments.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Will you guys do anything for the community center?

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: Yeah, I can add to that.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: So those are, as Eva mentioned, the direct allocations from city council members, other elected officials are going directly to older adult center comprehensive renovations.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: We have completed seven of those, primarily city discretionary funded in the last year and a half.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: We have 16 active projects with a total budget of $57 million, and we have six planned that are currently in discussion around funding.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: So across those completed active planned, that covers about 30 of our Section 9 older adult centers currently in our portfolio.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: But that is separate from the...

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: The city funding that you mentioned, the city funding lines that you mentioned.

chapters.summary: Zhuang notes the FY27 executive budget added $20 million for critical repair initiative and $10 million for mold and leak complaints. She asks if that money can be used for Latimer Gardens OAC. Trimble says no, those allocations are for apartment repairs, not OAC capital improvements. Zhuang says it does not make sense given earlier testimony.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks if critical repair initiative can fund Latimer Gardens OAC

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, similarly in FY27 executive budget, the administration added 20 million FY27 to FY30 for critical repair initiative, and 10 million over this year, and then

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: next year to addressing long outstanding mold and leak complaints.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Is this money able to use for the Timir Garden OAC, this type of repair?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: No, those allocations, which we're very grateful for, are significant funding that's going to help us make progress on old repairs, both mold and leaks and others, in apartments.

chapters.summary: Zhuang says it seems NYCHA has nothing allocated to older adult centers in its budget. Trimble says OAC allocations are discretionary from elected officials, and NYCHA's priority is resident apartments. Zhuang says that contradicts earlier statements about repairing leaks at senior centers. Trimble clarifies repairs are different from capital improvements.
chapters.title: Zhuang presses on NYCHA budget for older adult centers

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So in Niche's budget, there's nothing allocated to older adult center.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: The older adult center allocations are the discretionary allocations of the elected officials.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We are focused primarily, our priority is to resolve conditions in resident apartments, and we are putting our funding towards those priorities right now.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So that doesn't make sense to me.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: You said in the beginning of testimony, you said, well, we're going to do the repairs.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Like some senior center has some leaks.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Now you say, oh, we have money, we cannot.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Let me clarify, Council Member.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Repairs are different from capital improvements.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So the funding that you're talking about right now are primarily capital improvements.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: The mold and leaks and the critical repairs initiatives are special allocations we received from this administration to focus on very old apartment conditions, and those are repairs.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: And the other pots of funding you were talking about were capital improvements.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: So we will continue to respond to repairs.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: in older adult centers, when we get the work orders, we respond to them, but we don't have a specific funding source dedicated to that repair.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So you can do the repair for the older adult senior center, but you cannot do repair for Latimer Garden OAC.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: But Latimer Gardens requires a capital improvement.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: It's not about a repair.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: But it's leaking.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Start with leaking.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: It's leaking from the roof.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: The roof needs to be repaired, and that's a significant capital.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We are working with funders right now to hopefully get funding for that roof capital project.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: But if it's...

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: They have leaking, you repair it right away.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: It should not become a huge issue.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: That's always happening in OACs.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We get complaints all the time.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Yes, we have significant infrastructure challenges.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: We will repair a leak, and the leak will come back in a different part of the pipe, or we'll patch up the roof.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: But we're talking about a roof that's probably past its useful life and needs a capital...

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: A capital project, a new roof, not just continuing to patch and band-aid the old holes in that roof.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: That is why the leaks keep coming back.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, there's no plan, say, every 20 years or 30 years the roof have be updated.

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: Unfortunately, NYCHA's apartments, let alone their older adult centers, are not capitalized with ongoing funds.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: So who is responsible for that?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: The federal, state, or city?

utterances.speaker: Eva Trimble
utterances.text: I would say all of the above.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks what DFTA's capital budget allocation was for NYCHA this year. McKenzie says DFTA does not have a capital budget and does not affect capital projects on its own. Projects come from elected officials or discretionary funds. Zhuang asks how much DFTA allocated to NYCHA OACs for capital; McKenzie says DFTA only covers minor repairs.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about DFTA capital budget for NYCHA OACs

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And what's a DIFTA capital?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: budget allocated was NITRA this year?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: DIFTA does not have a capital budget.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: It is something because we don't affect any capital projects on our own.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: The projects that we've completed are in consultation with or

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: have come from funding that comes from either elected officials or discretionary funds.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Sorry, I mean the improvement you guys with CD give the money, how much you guys allocated to nature related?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: OACs for capital.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: As I mentioned, we're only covering minor repairs, so it would come through the budgets at the individual site for us to be able to repair something that's very, very minor.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: If it's larger than that, then we're working on projects that have been funded separately.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Let's switch the gear.

chapters.summary: Zhuang shifts to Intro 1083 and asks what financial support DFTA currently offers older adults. McKenzie says DFTA has several programs for long-term care planning, protecting retirement funds, and preventing fraud and scams. She agrees with the intent of having a financial literacy advisor at every site but needs to review implications and cost.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks what financial support DFTA currently offers older adults

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: We have some questions about YINCHO 1083.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: What financial support does DFTA currently offer older adults in New York City?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Are there any programs currently?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: I know you mentioned that you have one program before.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Well, we have several programs that help train our older New Yorkers and provide assistance to them for

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: long-term care planning and things like that, as you mentioned, that can help them to protect their funds in retirement and also just to protect

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: them from being defrauded and scammed and so on.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So we do have some of those programs available now.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We do also agree with the intent of having a financial literacy advisor at every one of the sites.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We just need to review the implications of that.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: What would it take to actually provide that at all of the sites and what would be the cost?

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks if DFTA case managers are already equipped to assist older adults with financial concerns or if the bill would require new staff or training. McKenzie says it would probably require someone new because finance is a specific discipline. Case managers can help find programs but typically are not financial experts.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks if case managers could serve as financial literacy advisors

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And are DIFTA case managers already equipped to assist older adults with financial concerns?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And assume the role of financial literacy advisor or would pass, could pass this bill require further training or hire new staff?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: In my opinion at this moment, while we're still negotiating and reviewing, I would say it probably would be someone new because, you know, finance is, you know, a very specific discipline.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: It's not something that normally a case manager would be well versed in.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: They could help you to be able to find certain programs that they could sign up for and services across the city.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: But typically that's not the role of a case manager.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks what implementation of Intro 1083 could look like financially and how much it would increase costs per OAC. McKenzie says preliminary numbers put it at about $2 to $3 million to roll out across all sites, but they are not confirmed and are still reviewing.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about cost to implement Intro 1083

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: What does the DIFTA imagine implement this bill could look like?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Like financially, how much do you think is going to increase for each OACs?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We have some preliminary numbers that put us at about between $2 to $3 million to roll it out across all sites.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: They're not confirmed, and we're still...

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: reviewing.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So as you mentioned, imagining, that's exactly where we are right now.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We're imagining what it would take for us to be able to do this.

chapters.summary: Zhuang asks if there is another way to help seniors if DFTA cannot place a financial literacy advisor in each center. McKenzie says perhaps; they could have someone move between sites or share an advisor among centers, similar to mobile geriatric mental health services. They need to review all options.
chapters.title: Zhuang asks about alternatives if each center cannot have an advisor

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: If you are not able to have each delicate person in each center, is there any other way you guys can help those seniors?

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: We do provide training, as I mentioned before, so it could be possible to have someone that could move between sites, as I mentioned about the mobile geriatric mental health services that we're looking to.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: There could be a way to have certain centers share.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: Financial literacy advisor.

utterances.speaker: Lisa Scott McKenzie
utterances.text: So we have to review all options and find out what would be the most responsible thing for us to do.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: And Chair Banks has a couple more questions.

chapters.summary: Banks says a briefing suggested giving money to the sponsor because NYCHA is slow on capital improvements. He asks if that would work better. Fradkin says for substantial capital work, NYCHA prefers to manage it, and capital work typically takes about four years due to design and procurement. Banks says some repairs have taken longer and are dire.
chapters.title: Banks asks if capital funds could go to sponsors instead of NYCHA

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: On the side of the capital side, I know...

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: A briefing that I had with the capital improvements team at NYCHA, it was suggested that, well, we know that NYCHA is pretty slow when it comes to,

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I guess, bringing down the money or making capital improvements.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Sometimes it can take years.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: It was suggested that we give money to the sponsor.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Is that something you would suggest or you think would work better since NITRA hasn't been

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: as efficient, but making those capital investments to the out centers.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: For any substantial capital work, NITCHA, you know, if it's a major capital renovation to the space, upgrades to the building system, NITCHA,

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: would prefer to manage that work.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: Any capital work is necessarily typically an average of four years because there is an extensive school design process.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: But it seems like it's taken longer than even the timeline that you just mentioned.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And some of these, you know, some of the repairs and the things that are needed are dire.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And some of these centers, it's been going on for years, on top of years.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: I mean, if NYCHA is not able to do it, would it be okay that we give it to a sponsor or the sponsor of the development or, I mean, of that particular center or the CBO?

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: If you have particular examples, we're happy to work with you to kind of identify the best way forward.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: Typically, our providers are not able to manage capital work themselves.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: And so that is why NYCHA manages the work once full funding is allocated.

chapters.summary: Banks says many centers are not ADA accessible and asks if giving money to a sponsor would be faster and more efficient. Fradkin says if the work rises to capital level, such as making bathrooms or spaces wheelchair accessible with structural changes, NYCHA would manage it. A ramp outside the center might be covered by the provider.
chapters.title: Banks asks if sponsors could handle ADA accessibility projects faster

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: And the reason why I say that, because I know that it was said that the ADA accessibility, a lot of the centers are not ADA accessible.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Is that a project you think we should be better served if we were able to give the monies to a sponsor and it would be done much quicker?

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: Efficient.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: It depends on the level of work that is needed.

utterances.speaker: Chris Banks
utterances.text: So all seniors, all older adults can be able to have access to these government-funded centers.

utterances.speaker: Abigail Fradkin
utterances.text: If the work that's needed rises to the level of capital work, so making the bathrooms or other spaces wheelchair accessible or accessible in other major ways that require

chapters.summary: Bridget Lee testifies on behalf of the Weinberg Center for Elder Justice, which serves older adults experiencing mistreatment and financial exploitation. She supports Intro 1083 and says financial security is an elder justice issue. She urges the council to strengthen the bill by requiring advisor training in elder abuse, financial exploitation, scam intervention, and consultation with elder justice providers.
chapters.title: Bridget Lee testifies for Weinberg Center for Elder Justice on Intro 1083

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: My name is Bridget Lee, and I'm here on behalf of the Weinberg Center for Elder Justice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: We are a multidisciplinary team of attorneys, social workers, medical professionals, and public health specialists who have spent more than two decades serving older adults experiencing mistreatment, including financial exploitation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: In addition to operating the nation's first elder abuse shelter, we provide comprehensive direct services and conduct extensive outreach and training, much of it focused on scam prevention, financial security, and preventing exploitation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: We thank the council and the committees for their attention to the financial well-being of older New Yorkers, and we support Intro 1083.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: Financial security is not only an economic issue, but an elder justice issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: More than one in five older New Yorkers live in poverty, and many more live on fixed incomes with no room to absorb a loss.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: In NYCHA, 45% of all households are headed by someone 62 or older.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: For these residents, a single scam or an exploitative family member can mean losing their housing, their medication, or their next meal.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: Financial exploitation is the most common form of elder abuse in New York State, occurring at a rate of 41 per 1,000 older adults, yet only 1 in 24 cases of elder abuse is ever reported to a government agency or committee.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: community-based service provider.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: A New York State study of verified financial exploitation cases found that 67% of perpetrators were family members, most often adult children.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: The people most likely to take an older adult's money are often the very people they trust and depend on.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: Scams are a distinct but equally urgent threat.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: In 2025, Americans

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: Ages 60 and over reported almost $8 billion in losses to the FBI, a nearly 60% increase from the year before, with an average loss of $38K per person.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: While scams differ from abuse by family members or caregivers, they often rely on the same emotional manipulation.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: Scammers fabricate relationships posing as a romantic partner, a grandchild in trouble, or a trusted official, and they prey on social isolation and so many older adults'experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: They prey on the social isolation so many older adults experience.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: In our work, we see that financial instability is frequently the first visible sign of abuse.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: An unpaid bill, a sudden change to a bank account, or a new name on a power of attorney can signal that something is wrong.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: A financial literacy advisor sitting with an older adult to review a budget or plan for end of life may be the first person to notice and the first person the older adult trusts enough to tell.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: That is why we urge the council to strengthen Intro 1083 in four ways.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: First, require that the advisor training program include elder abuse and financial exploitation, which include the red flags, the dynamics of exploitation by family members and caregivers, and how to respond safely when an older adult discloses harm.

utterances.speaker: Council Staff
utterances.text: Okay, can you wrap that up?

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Or you can submit to the written testimony.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: Second, we would just require that advisors be trained in scam intervention strategies.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: Third, we would name elder abuse service providers among the contacts advisors share to older adults.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Bridget Lee
utterances.text: And fourth, we would direct DIFTA to consult with elder justice providers in developing advisor qualifications in training.

chapters.summary: Anita Kwok, policy analyst at United Neighborhood Houses, says many member OACs in NYCHA facilities face unresolved repairs and unclear site control. Providers must choose between paying for repairs without resources or chasing NYCHA contacts. She calls for a strong interagency approach, leases that fairly divide responsibilities, and dedicated capital funding.
chapters.title: Anita Kwok testifies on NYCHA OAC repair and site control issues

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: Hello, thank you, Councilmember Drong, for the opportunity to testify.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: My name is Anita Kwok.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: I am a policy analyst at United Neighborhood Houses.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: Many of our members run OACs and NITRA facilities that deal with a bunch of challenges, such as unresolved repairs and unclear site control.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: So from plumbing to kitchen equipment to electric...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: To electrical work, providers have to choose between paying for repairs without the resources to do so, or spending countless hours chasing a contact at NYCHA that could possibly help them with their issue.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: Even if a provider has outside resources and the ability to conduct major capital improvements, the unclear or total lack of site control slows down or makes these efforts impossible.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: Solving these challenges requires a strong interagency approach with NYCHA and NYC Aging, but we do not believe that this relationship has materialized in practice.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: In our experience, NYC Aging and NYCHA often defer these responsibilities to each other without a solution in sight.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: Our members question if a NYCHA liaison exists, and there's often no resolution for the tickets that they submit to NYCHA.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: Sometimes

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: Projects have been paused for years due to lack of funding, and that leaves OACs without operating, without critical systems.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: This poor bureaucratic process leads to a prolonged repair timelines and uncertainty for providers to serve older adults safely.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: Site control issues are also a huge barrier to resolving repair needs in NYCHA community spaces.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: Our members have been asked to take on responsibilities such as extermination or signing leases without city funding to cover rent, even though rent is an...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: An allowable cost under most human services contracts.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: Providers cannot be expected to assume significant maintenance at a site that they do not control and have the funding to maintain.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: As a landlord, NYCHA is responsible for OACs and should pay for routine maintenance and services such as extermination, particularly because OACs also serve the older adults in NYCHA facilities.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: I also...

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: Want to say that a first step towards resolving community needs in NYCHA community spaces is ensuring that every human service organization operating in a NYCHA facility has a lease, and these leases must fairly divide the responsibilities between the provider and NYCHA,

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: and most crucially include funding for the rent from the service contracting agency like NYC Aging.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: Without addressing this underlying issue, capital needs in NYCHA spaces will go unresolved for years.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: And lastly, I

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: want to add that a dedicated funding stream for fully funded capital services is really important and we thank you for your advocacy in the

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Anita Kwok
utterances.text: past budget year for the expansion of a capital fund at OACs, and we look forward to doing it with you next year.

utterances.speaker: Susan Zhuang
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosemary Salazar

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosemary Salazar

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosemary Salazar

utterances.speaker: Member of the Public - Rosemary Salazar

summary: Joint hearing of the Committee on Public Housing and Committee on Aging on older adult centers at NYCHA facilities and Intro 1083 on financial literacy advisors.
Providers testified about leaks, mold, HVAC failures, unclear repair responsibilities, and RAD/PACT conversion challenges; NYCHA and DFTA described coordination but acknowledged capital funding gaps.

Council members questioned agencies on repair tickets, response times, ADA compliance, fines, and budget allocations; public witnesses supported Intro 1083 and raised fire panel and site control issues.
